documents: The study data were obtained from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) database and included both healthy controls (HC) and mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease (AD) participants.
The study compared standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics with an advanced free-water DTI (FW-DTI) model to remove the effects of extracellular free water (FW).

The study compared fractional anisotropy, axial diffusivity, radial diffusivity, and mean diffusivity from both standard DTI and FW-DTI between Alzheimer's disease and healthy control subjects using data from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) brain project.
The analysis investigated the FW index for both groups and performed voxel-based correlations between all DTI-derived metrics from DTI and FW-DTI and the mini-mental state examination (MMSE) score.

The study cohort comprised 30 healthy controls (17 female, mean age 73) and 28 Alzheimer's disease patients (15 female, mean age 75), with Alzheimer's disease patients exhibiting significantly lower MMSE scores and higher CDR scores than healthy controls.
The Alzheimer's disease group included 16 participants with CDR 0.5, 10 with CDR 1, 1 with CDR 2, and 1 with CDR 3, while all 30 healthy controls had a CDR score of 0.

The study utilized diffusion-based magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) analyzed with the diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) model to evaluate white matter integrity via fractional anisotropy, axial diffusivity, and radial diffusivity.

To mitigate partial volume effects caused by extracellular free water, the study applied a free water correction algorithm (FW-DTI) to quantify and remove the contribution of extracellular free water from DTI-derived metrics.
Free-water (FW)-corrected maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script, with the FW maps computed by fitting a specific model at each voxel.

The free-water model fitting used a b-value of 1000 s/mm² and set the diffusion coefficient for the isotropic free-water compartment to 3 × 10⁻³ mm²/s, representing the diffusivity of water at body temperature.

Standard DTI metrics were reported as axial diffusivity (AxD), radial diffusivity (RD), and fractional anisotropy (FA), while FW-corrected DTI metrics were reported as AxD_t, RD_t, and FA_t to indicate greater tissue specificity.
The study included 30 healthy controls and 28 Alzheimer's disease subjects, all aged between 60 and 90 years, who had 3 T dMRI data available with more than 30 directions.

Exclusion criteria for the study were cognitively impaired participants with dementia not attributed to Alzheimer's disease, healthy control participants with significant comorbidities, and participants for whom the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) was not available.

All diffusion MRI data were acquired using a 3 T Siemens scanner with 64 diffusion-encoding directions, a b value of 1000 s/mm², TR/TE of 11,000/87.0 ms, a flip angle of 90°, a matrix of 96×96, a field of view of 24.0 × 24.0 cm, a slice thickness of 2.5 mm, and 64 axial slices.

The dMRI data were preprocessed using the FMRIB software library (FSL) version 5.0.4, which included eddy current and motion correction and compensation of gradient orientations for rotational components.
A brain mask for each subject was defined using the Brain Extraction Toolbox (BET) for the single B0 images, and DTI standard and FW-corrected maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script.

The study used standard DTI metrics, including fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AxD), and radial diffusivity (RD), to analyze differences between healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) groups.
The statistical analysis for the standard DTI metrics was an ANCOVA with a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for family-wise error (FWE).

B0 images from each subject were used to create a B0 groupwise template image using the buildtemplateparallel.sh script included in ANTs, and the B0 group-wise template image was subsequently normalized to the IIT_mean_b0 image by the ANTs symmetric image normalization (SyN) algorithm.

The warp fields obtained from the normalization and B0 group-wise template creation were used to transfer all DTI maps to the Illinois Institute of Technology (IIT) Human Brain Atlas (v.4.1) in International Consortium for Brain Mapping (ICBM)-152 space.
All DTI maps in standard space were smoothed using FSL with an isotropic Gaussian kernel with a sigma of 3 mm.

Comparisons of all DTI-, FW-DTI- metrics, and FW maps between groups were performed using the FSL Randomise tool with threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) and a correction for multiple comparisons via Family-Wise Error (FWE) rate at a 0.01 level.
A white matter mask was defined using a threshold of 0.2 on the average values of fractional anisotropy (FA) from standard DTI and was applied to the other DTI maps.
For each voxel, the DTI-derived metrics were fitted by an Analysis of Covariance model (ANCOVA) which included age and sex as covariates, with the number of randomized permutations set at 5,000.
The clusters identified to be statistically different between groups were labeled according to the Johns Hopkins University (JHU) DTI-based white-matter atlases.

For the cognitively impaired group (AD only), the voxel-based relationship between MMSE scores and DTI metrics was assessed through FSL Randomise with significance at a p-value < 0.01, corrected for Family-Wise Error (FWE).

The study applied a False Discovery Rate (FWE) correction threshold of p<0.01 to the fractional anisotropy (FA_t), axial diffusivity (AxD_t), and radial diffusivity (RD_t) metrics, while a less stringent p<0.05 FWE corrected threshold was applied to a specific cluster in the body of the corpus callosum showing higher RD_t values.

The statistical analysis identified significant differences in fractional anisotropy (FA_t), axial diffusivity (AxD_t), and radial diffusivity (RD_t) between the Alzheimer's disease (AD) and healthy control (HC) groups, with specific volume percentages reported for the affected clusters in the fornix and corpus callosum.

The study compared standard DTI and Free-water DTI (FW-DTI) metrics, including the FW index derived from the fit in Equation 1, to identify significant differences between Alzheimer's disease (AD) and healthy control (HC) groups.
Statistical significance for the group differences in the FW index was determined using a threshold of p < 0.01 with Family Wise Error (FWE) correction.
The analysis utilized two specific white-matter atlases for regional definitions: the JHU white-matter tractography atlas and the ICBM-DTI-81 white-matter atlas.

All reported cluster results were based on a significance threshold of p < 0.01 with Family Wise Error (FWE) correction, except for the specific RD (HC) < RD (AD) comparison which was reported at p < 0.05 with FWE correction.
The study utilized two white matter atlases for analysis: the JHU WM tract atlas and the ICBM-DTI-81 WM atlas.
Figure 4 presents an ANCOVA analysis between Healthy Control (HC) and Alzheimer's Disease (AD) subjects for the Mean Anisotropy (MA) index derived from both standard DTI and FW-DTI methods.
The statistical significance threshold for the ANCOVA analysis shown in Figure 4 was a p-value < 0.01 corrected for Family Wise Error (FWE).

The ANCOVA analysis between healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) subjects for FW-DTI metrics reported clusters at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for False Discovery Rate (FWE), with the exception of the radial diffusivity (RD_t) comparison which used a p-value < 0.05 FWE-corrected threshold.

The ANCOVA analysis between healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) subjects for the Fiber Weight (FW) index reported clusters at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for False Discovery Rate (FWE).
Clusters of significant differences between groups for the mean anisotropy (MA) index analysis were reported at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for family-wise error (FWE).
The study utilized the JHU white-matter tractography atlas and the ICBM-DTI-81 white-matter atlas to define brain locations for the mean anisotropy (MA) index analysis.

No significant voxel-based correlation was found between the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and either standard or fiber-orientation (FW)-corrected diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics at the p < 0.05 family-wise error (FWE) corrected level.

Correlations between fractional anisotropy (FA) and axial diffusivity (AxD) or radial diffusivity (RD) were calculated for healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) groups, showing increased correlation coefficients after fiber-orientation (FW) correction.

White matter integrity was assessed using both standard and free-water (FW) corrected diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics in participants with Alzheimer's disease and healthy controls. The study incorporated a free-water component into the conventional diffusion modeling pipeline to remove free-water-contaminated voxels and mitigate partial volume effects, producing FW-corrected DTI metrics and a complementary free-water index.

The study compared standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) with free water diffusion tensor imaging (FW-DTI) to assess white matter integrity in Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients compared to healthy controls.

The free water (FW) volume fraction was quantified using the FW-correction algorithm, which revealed higher FW values in the AD group across multiple white matter areas, including the cingulum, inferior longitudinal fasciculus, and corpus callosum.

The study analyzed voxel-wise correlations between diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics and the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) in the Alzheimer's disease (AD) cohort, finding no significant correlations before or after free water (FW) correction.
The study applied fractional anisotropy (FA) correction to diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics to improve accuracy and sensitivity in Alzheimer's disease (AD) participants.

The study utilized skeletonized tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) to identify FA reductions in the fornix in early-symptomatic individuals and those at high risk for developing Alzheimer's disease.
The study used both standard and FW-DTI methods to observe large clusters of lower FA in the genu and body of the corpus callosum (CC) in Alzheimer's disease participants.
The study employed standard DTI methods that assume Gaussian diffusion within the tensor model, which creates an inability to resolve different fiber orientations within a voxel.
The study used mean anisotropy (MA) as a metric of diffusion anisotropy to provide insight in areas with crossing fibers and complicated tract topologies in Alzheimer's disease subjects.

The study used a voxel-based approach for white matter analysis rather than a skeletonized approach like TBSS, a choice that may increase sensitivity to subtle differences in microstructure but relies on atlases that covered only 84% of the white matter mask.

The study did not observe significant voxel-based correlations (p<0.01 FWE corrected) between standard DTI and FW-DTI metrics and the MMSE score, suggesting a non-linear relationship between global cognitive scores and white matter pathology.
The study implemented a FW correction algorithm for DTI to improve the sensitivity and specificity of derived DTI metrics by removing partial volume effects.
The study was conducted by researchers from the Division of Neuroimaging Research and the Muhammad Ali Parkinson Center at the Barrow Neurological Institute in Phoenix, AZ, USA.
The study data was provided by the OASIS project, which was supported by NIH Grants P50 AG05681, P01 AG03991, R01 AG021910, P50 MH071616, U24 RR021382, and R01 MH56584.
The study utilized the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS) database, which provides longitudinal MRI data for nondemented and demented older adults.
The study employed the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) as a practical method for grading the cognitive state of patients.
The study applied FSL (FMRIB Software Library) for functional and structural MR image analysis.
The study used an integrated approach to correct for off-resonance effects and subject movement in diffusion MR imaging.
The study performed fast robust automated brain extraction using the method described by Smith (2002).
The study utilized orthogonal tensor invariants for the analysis of diffusion tensor magnetic resonance images.
The study emphasized the importance of group-wise registration in tract-based spatial statistics studies of neurodegeneration.
The study used symmetric diffeomorphic image registration with cross-correlation for automated labeling.
The study utilized a high angular resolution diffusion imaging human brain template developed by Varentsova et al.
The study applied permutation inference for the general linear model for statistical analysis.
The study used threshold-free cluster enhancement to address problems of smoothing, threshold dependence, and localisation in cluster inference.
The study utilized tract probability maps in stereotaxic spaces for white matter anatomy analysis and tract-specific quantification.
The study applied quantitative tractography methods to cerebral white matter, noting their reproducibility.

The study utilized a 3T scanner with 1.5mm isotropic resolution but failed to specify slice timing, a methodological omission that could introduce temporal artifacts into the BOLD signal preprocessing pipeline.

The study selected eighteen participants diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment at baseline and Alzheimer's disease at follow-up from the AD Neuroimaging Initiative for a 2-year longitudinal analysis.
Tract-based spatial statistics was used to assess longitudinal changes in white matter, with voxel-wise and region-of-interest analyses conducted.
Statistical models controlled for age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status.

The study utilizes diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to detect microstructural changes and white matter tract integrity, relying on the principle that water diffusion aligns with fiber tract orientation and that damage reduces this anisotropy.

The study employs axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) as DTI metrics, where AxD represents the rate of water diffusion along the principal eigenvector (λ1) and RD reflects the rate of water diffusion along the two axes orthogonal to λ1.

The study uses longitudinal DTI analyses to examine the temporal dynamics of white matter degeneration and its role in clinical deterioration during the transition from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease.

The study utilized data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database, specifically selecting 18 participants diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) at baseline who progressed to Alzheimer's disease (AD) at the 2-year follow-up.

Longitudinal changes in axonal damage (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) were evaluated using tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) implemented with the FMRIB Software Library (FSL) over a 2-year period.

Follow-up assessments were conducted at 24.78 ± 1.75 months after the baseline assessment, and participants with missing baseline or follow-up diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) images were excluded from the final analysis.
A general linear model was incorporated into the TBSS framework with age, sex, education, and APOE epsilon 4 status as independent variables and AxD/RD as the dependent variable.
Spearman's correlation analysis was used to examine changes in ROI-based AxD, RD, and CDR while controlling for age, sex, education, APOE epsilon 4 status, and baseline CDR score.
Uncorrected P-values were reported for correlation analyses because applying the Bonferroni correction to the small sample size would have significantly lowered statistical power.
A post hoc power analysis was conducted using G*Power version 3.1 to evaluate the adequacy of the sample size in detecting meaningful correlations.

Multiple linear regression analysis was performed with the change in CDR scores as the dependent variable and AxD and RD as independent variables, treating age, sex, education, APOE epsilon 4 status, and baseline CDR score as confounders.
Multivariate regression analysis was conducted independently for each WM region that showed notable variations in AxD or RD in the TBSS analysis.

Demographic and clinical characteristics were compared between the included group (n=18) and the excluded group (n=44) to assess potential sample bias due to exclusion of participants with missing DTI data.

The study used FSL to register fractional anisotropy maps to an FA template space (FMRIB58_FA 1 x 1 x 1 mm) created using the FA maps of the 18 participants in the study. A mean FA skeleton was constructed by averaging the FA maps, and a threshold of 0.2 was applied to refine the skeleton to include only voxels with sufficient FA values.

The Johns Hopkins University white-matter tractography atlas was used to conduct region-of-interest analysis on the cingulum, corpus callosum, and uncinate fasciculus to extract AxD and RD values. These ROI analyses were conducted in an exploratory, post hoc manner based on regions showing significant differences in the TBSS whole-brain analysis, rather than on a priori hypotheses.

All statistical analyses were conducted using Jamovi version 2.3.28.0 and FSL version 6.0.6. Longitudinal differences in AxD and RD values were analyzed using TBSS with permutation-based statistical testing.

Permutation testing with 5,000 iterations was used to generate a null distribution of t-values by randomly rearranging the data among the participants. A threshold-free cluster enhancement method was applied within the permutation-based paired t-tests to correct for multiple comparisons at the voxel level, with statistical significance set at P < 0.05.

A general linear model was incorporated into the TBSS framework to account for potential confounding factors, with age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status as independent variables and AxD or RD as the dependent variable.
The study included 18 participants with a mean age of 72.00 ± 8.69 years, of whom 6 (33.33%) were female.
Participants were classified as apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 carriers if they had one or more APOE ε4 alleles, and as non-carriers if they had no APOE ε4 alleles.
The requirement for written informed consent was waived by the Institutional Review Board of Gachon University (1044396-202405-HR-086-01).

Participants were classified into cognitively normal, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's disease (AD) groups at both time points based on clinical dementia rating (CDR) scores in accordance with the ADNI criteria.
Cognitive decline was defined as the change in the clinical dementia rating (CDR) scores over the 2-year period, calculated as the CDR at follow-up minus the CDR at baseline.
Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) data were acquired using a 3T MRI scanner following detailed imaging protocols described in publicly available documents.
FSL version 6.0.6 and MRtrix3 were used to correct DTI artifacts, including noise, Gibbs artifacts, eddy current-induced distortions, and bias field inhomogeneity.
The diffusion tensor model was fitted using "dtifit" in FSL to generate λ1 (L1), λ2 (L2), and λ3 (L3) maps.
Axial diffusivity (AxD) was determined using the primary eigenvalue (λ1), while radial diffusivity (RD) was derived by averaging the secondary eigenvalues (λ2 and λ3).
The study utilized the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score as the metric for cognitive decline to correlate with white matter integrity.
The statistical analysis for the correlation between white matter integrity and cognitive decline applied family-wise error (FWE) correction.

The study employed tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) to analyze axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) changes, using a family-wise error (FWE) correction for multiple comparisons at a significance threshold of P<0.05.

The statistical analysis identified significant changes in white matter microstructure over a two-year follow-up period, with specific voxel counts reported for regions such as the superior longitudinal fasciculus and posterior corona radiata.
The study cohort consisted of 18 participants (6 female, 12 male) with a mean baseline age of 72.00 years (SD 8.69) and a mean baseline Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) of 2.42 (SD 1.17).
Participants were classified as APOE ε4 carriers if they had one or more APOE ε4 alleles, with 6 of the 18 participants (33.33%) identified as carriers and 12 (66.67%) as non-carriers.

The study utilized Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS) analysis to evaluate white matter integrity, revealing significant increases in axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) values at follow-up compared to baseline.

The study longitudinally evaluated white matter microstructure by analyzing diffusion metrics AxD and RD, which are anisotropic diffusion metrics measured using DTI and sensitive to microstructural barriers like cell membranes and myelin sheaths.

The study used TBSS analysis to reveal significant changes in AxD and RD across the corpus callosum (CC), cingulum (CR), cingulate gyrus (CG), superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF), inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF), and internal capsule (IC).

The study conducted a post hoc power analysis using G*Power version 3.1 with a sample size of N=18 and an alpha level of 0.05. The analysis indicated 93.7% power to detect a correlation of r=0.704 and 86.3% power for the average observed correlation of r=0.644 across significant regions.

The researchers performed multiple linear regression analyses with Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) changes as the dependent variable, adjusting for age, APOE epsilon 4 status, education, sex, and baseline CDR. The regression analysis included regions of interest exhibiting significant differences in both axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) values from the Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS) analysis.
The study used multivariate regression analysis to investigate the separate effects of AxD and RD changes on clinical progression.

The lack of significant RD-CDR associations may be attributed to technical limitations such as the spatial resolution of DTI and the skeleton-based nature of TBSS, which may hinder the detection of subtle peripheral WM changes.

The study was a longitudinal investigation examining the relationship between white matter microstructural changes assessed using diffusion metrics, including axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD), and cognitive decline during the progression from mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to Alzheimer's disease (AD).
The study utilized multivariate regression analysis to evaluate the relationship between AxD and RD changes in white matter regions of interest and changes in Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores.
The study longitudinally analyzed the progression from Mild Cognitive Impairment to Alzheimer's Disease to evaluate microstructural changes in white matter integrity.
The study had a small sample size of n=18, which limits the generalizability of the findings and reduces statistical power.
The study reported uncorrected p-values due to the small sample size, acknowledging the risk of inflated false-positive rates.

The Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS) analysis focused only on the core regions of the white matter tract by projecting the highest fractional anisotropy values onto the alignment-invariant tract representation (the FA skeleton).
Cognitive function was evaluated exclusively using Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores, which lack detailed assessment of various cognitive domains.
Region of interest (ROI) analyses were conducted post hoc based on TBSS findings, which may raise concerns about circular reasoning.
APOE ε4 status was included as a covariate in all statistical models, but potential interaction effects between ε4 status and white matter changes were not tested.

The analysis relied on FWE-corrected p<0.05 for MMSE correlations but omitted effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals, a reporting gap that prevents distinguishing clinically meaningful Free Water shifts from noise and leaves the multiple comparison correction strategy for regional testing ambiguous.
The study enrolled 43 patients with Alzheimer's disease and 16 healthy controls, all of whom underwent diffusion spectrum imaging (DSI) and conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

The acquired images were processed to obtain diffusion MRI models and multiparameter values, with Pearson correlation analysis used to assess relationships between diffusion parameters and clinical cognitive scores.

Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was conducted to evaluate the diagnostic performance of diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI), and mean apparent propagator (MAP) parameters.

The study utilizes diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) to sensitize the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) signal to water molecule diffusion, specifically employing diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) as the primary model for studying white matter changes in Alzheimer's disease.

The study employs neurite Orientation Density and Dispersion Imaging (NODDI), a biophysical-based diffusion-weighted imaging model that assumes the signal emanates from three distinct tissue compartments: within neurites, outside of neurites, and free water.

The primary parameters derived from the NODDI model used in the study are intracellular volume fraction (ICVF), extracellular volume fraction (ECVF), isotropic volume fraction (ISOVF), and orientation dispersion index (ODI).

The study combined NODDI, MAP-MRI, and DTI models to investigate Alzheimer's disease-related microstructural changes and assess correlations between diffusivity and cognitive function measured by Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores.
The study assessed the diagnostic performance of different diffusion MRI parameters using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.
The diffusion MRI models were concurrently obtained from diffusion spectral imaging (DSI), a grid acquisition model that reconstructs diverse diffusion MRI models via raw diffusion data.

The study acquired a total of 128 diffusion sampling points, comprising 24 directions at b=3000 s/mm² and 3 directions at b=3000 s/mm², with a total scan time of approximately 10 minutes and 8 seconds.

Diffusion data analysis was performed using in-house prototype software developed by MR Station (Chengdu Zhongying Medical Technology Co., Ltd.), after converting raw data to NIFTI format, applying eddy current correction with FSL, and denoising with a Gaussian filter with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 3 mm.
Three diffusion models—DTI, MAP-MRI, and NODDI—were fitted to the processed data to derive related diffusion metrics and quantitative microstructural parameter maps.

The study enrolled 43 patients with mild cognitive impairment or dementia due to probable Alzheimer's disease and 16 healthy controls, with healthy controls required to have no evidence of cognitive impairment, an MMSE score of 25 or higher, a MoCA score of 25 or higher, and a CDR score of 0.

Participants were excluded from the study if they had severe cerebrovascular disorder, severe white matter hyperintensity, a history of psychiatric illness or severe injury, used medications that influence cognition, were left-handed, had contraindications to MRI, or had poor-quality MRI images due to movement artifacts.

All participants underwent a DSI sequence on a 3.0T MRI scanner (Skyra; Siemens Healthcare, Erlangen, Germany) equipped with a 32-channel head coil, using an axial plane and half q-space Cartesian grid sampling procedure.

The DSI sequence acquisition parameters included a TR/TE of 4400/108 ms, a field of view of 220 x 220 mm², an SMS factor of 2, a slice thickness of 2.0 mm, a voxel size of 2.0 x 2.0 x 2.0 mm³, 60 slices, and a total scan time of approximately 10 minutes and 8 seconds.

The diffusion sampling comprised 128 directions across specific b-values: 0 volumes at b=0 s/mm², 3 directions at b=200 s/mm², 1 direction at b=350 s/mm², 5 directions at b=400 s/mm², 4 directions at b=550 s/mm², 3 directions at b=750 s/mm², 12 directions at b=950 s/mm², 12 directions at b=1150 s/mm², 6 directions at b=1500 s/mm², 15 directions at b=1700 s/mm², 1 direction at b=1850 s/mm², 11 directions at b=1900 s/mm², 12 directions at b=2050 s/mm², 4 directions at b=2250 s/mm², 12 directions at b=2450 s/mm², 24 directions at b=2650 s/mm², and 3 directions at b=3000 s/mm².

The study included 43 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients and 16 healthy volunteers (HC). The AD group had a significantly higher average age and significantly lower years of education, MMSE scores, and MoCA scores compared to the HC group, with no significant difference in gender between the two groups.

The analysis used a multivariate binary logistic regression model to evaluate diffusion parameters against AD, adjusting for the square of age, gender, and years of education. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, with sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and area under the curve (AUC) calculated using SPSS software.
Statistical significance was set at p<0.05, and a false discovery rate (FDR) was used to correct for multiple comparisons in the analysis of clinical cognitive scores and diffusion parameter values.

The disparity between patients with Alzheimer's Disease and healthy controls was assessed by processing diffusion parameter maps via a tract-based spatial statistics pipeline within the FSL toolbox from the Oxford Centre for Functional MRI of the Brain.

Fractional anisotropy maps for Alzheimer's Disease and healthy controls were nonlinearly registered to the FMRIB58_FA template, followed by affine alignment transformations into the 1 x 1 x 1 mm^2 Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI152) standard space.

The aligned images were averaged, skeletonized, and a mean fractional anisotropy skeleton was created, onto which the fractional anisotropy maps and other parameter maps of each subject were projected.
The whole brain was separated into 50 brain regions by employing the Johns Hopkins University (JHU)-White Matter-labels as masks.
Nonparametric permutation tests were carried out using the randomize tool with the number of random permutations set to 5000 to analyze group differences.
Threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) was utilized for multiple comparison correction with a statistical threshold defined as p < 0.001.
Statistical analyses were conducted using the IBM SPSS 23.0 software package (IBM Corp, Armonk, NY, USA).

Pearson correlation analysis was implemented to assess the relationship between clinical cognitive scores and diffusion parameter values, with a statistical significance criterion set at p < 0.05 and a false discovery rate (FDR) used to correct for multiple comparisons.

The diagnostic capabilities of diffusion parameters in six brain regions (splenium of the corpus callosum, fornix, cerebral peduncle R/L, anterior corona radiata R, and stria terminalis R) were evaluated using ROC curve analysis for the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease or mild cognitive impairment.

The study performed correlation analyses between DTI-derived parameters (AxD, FA, MD, RD), NODDI-derived parameters (ECVF, ICVF, ISOVF), MAP-MRI-derived parameters (MSD, QIV, NG, NGAx, NGRad, RTAP, RTOP, RTPP), and neuropsychological testing scores (MMSE, MoCA) in 25 AD patients.

The authors selected only specific brain regions and parameter values with good cognitive correlation for display because many parameter values of multiple brain regions were correlated with cognitive scale scores.

The study compared 43 Alzheimer's disease participants with 16 healthy controls, reporting demographic data such as age, gender, education, MMSE, and MoCA scores using mean ± standard deviation for normal distributions and median (interquartile range) for non-normal distributions.
MMSE and MoCA scores for the Alzheimer's disease group were reported based on a subset of 25 participants who had complete neuropsychologic data.

The imaging analysis utilized DTI parameters (axial diffusivity, fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity, radial diffusivity), NODDI parameters (extracellular volume fraction, intracellular volume fraction, isotropic volume fraction), and MAP-MRI parameters (mean-squared displacement, non-Gaussianity, axial non-Gaussianity, radial non-Gaussianity, q-space inverse variance, return-to-origin probability, return-to-axis probability, return-to-plane probability).

Statistical significance for the spatial distribution of diffusion parameters was defined as P < 0.001, with red indicating increased values and blue indicating decreased values in the Alzheimer's disease group relative to the healthy control group.
The study utilized advanced diffusion imaging models, specifically DTI, NODDI, and MAP-MRI, to assess white matter microstructural changes in Alzheimer's disease patients.

The diagnostic performance of diffusion imaging parameters was evaluated using ROC analysis, which reported AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, standardized beta coefficients, Z-scores, and FDR-corrected P-values.
Delong's test was used to compare the AUC of MAP-RTOP and NODDI-ECVF, revealing a significant difference with a Z-score of -2.217 and a p-value of 0.027.

The study utilized the NODDI model, which employs the Watson distribution for modeling, a methodological choice that may limit the accuracy of the Orientation Dispersion Index (ODI) in complex regions such as kissing fibers and crossing axons.

The study applied Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI), which assumes that the diffusion of water molecules in the brain follows a Gaussian distribution, a limitation that restricts the ability to detect diffusion heterogeneity in brain tissue.
The research involving human subjects was examined and approved by the Ethics Committee of Zigong First People's Hospital under protocol number Ethics(Reseach) No. 36, 2023.
The patients and participants in the study provided their written consent to participate.
The study lacked positron emission tomography (PET) examinations or pathologic verification to confirm tau protein deposition in participants with Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment.
The Alzheimer's disease groups in the study were not divided into various subtypes due to the relatively small sample size.

The analysis did not consider the presence of white matter hyperintensities (WMH), which may have influenced the results due to heterogeneous macrostructural white matter impairments across participants older than 60 years.

The study compared the diagnostic performance of DTI-derived RD/MD and NODDI-derived ISOVF/ECVF parameters using Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analysis and DeLong's test to assess statistical differences in Area Under the Curve (AUC) values.

The study utilized MAP-MRI parameters, specifically RTOP, QIV, MSD, and NGAx, to detect AD pathology and neurodegenerative changes, noting that these parameters characterize non-Gaussian diffusion profiles reflecting complex tissue organization.

The study evaluated the association between neuropsychologic scores and diffusion parameters from MAP-MRI, NODDI, and DTI models, finding that MAP-MRI parameters outperformed NODDI and DTI parameters in their correlation with cognitive function.

The study identified specific diffusion metrics, including RTOP, RTAP, ICVF, and FA, that showed meaningful correlations with MMSE and MoCA scores, with RTOP and RTAP exhibiting the most robust correlations with cognitive function.

The study utilized the standard Free-Water implementation within FSL’s EDIFY module but failed to specify the exact thresholding parameters for fiber orientation distribution estimation, creating a methodological ambiguity that obscures whether the observed 84% atlas coverage and smaller cluster sizes reflect biological reality or aggressive pipeline filtering.

The Free-Water model functions as a biophysical fit rather than a simple filter, yet the current paper fails to provide sensitivity analyses demonstrating that residual metrics remain stable across reasonable parameter variations, leaving the design's validity unverified.

Reproduction of the study is blocked by the absence of the specific FSL EDIFY software version and exact thresholding values, as the provided module name alone is insufficient to configure the baseline pipeline required for independent verification.
The study's generalizability is compromised by the exclusion of 44 participants with missing imaging, leaving a final sample of 18 whose specific exclusion criteria are undisclosed.
Reproduction of the analysis is blocked by the missing raw imaging data, the specific FSL EDIFY version, and the step-by-step processing log for the 18 remaining participants.

The analysis failed to account for white matter hyperintensities, a common comorbidity that acts as macrostructural noise and could explain the observed decline rather than validating the Free-Water method.

With a final sample size of n = 18, the study lacks the statistical power to detect true effects, and the absence of 95% confidence intervals on the Free-Water index renders the statistical support for the biophysical model unverifiable.

The Free-Water DTI studies utilize three distinct methodological frameworks with inconsistent parameter reporting, lacking harmonized data access, standardized software versions, and shared processing logs necessary for unified replication.

The Free-Water DTI studies define regions of interest (ROIs) based on initial findings, creating a circularity flaw where the same data used to generate the hypothesis is used to test it, rendering the anatomical localization speculative regardless of statistical corrections.

The analysis utilized post hoc regions of interest and uncorrected p-values, methodological parameters that create a high risk of false positives and undermine the validity of the specific anatomical localization claims.

The verification of the Free-Water DTI effects is currently blocked by missing specific software versions and thresholding details, which are necessary to determine if the signals are genuine biological changes or artifacts of aggressive data filtering.

The statistical analysis omitted the specific correction method for multiple comparisons, leaving the results based on an uncorrected family-wise error rate that prevents independent verification of the significance tests.
The pre-correction raw data and specific fitting constraints used in the Free-Water model were not provided, leaving only the final maps available for inspection.

The study design lacks a proper control group and independent validation, which creates a methodological bias where the Free-Water correction signal may represent algorithm overfitting to noise in a tiny sample rather than a biological effect.

The specific cognitive test battery used to derive the final CDR scores and the unprocessed raw diffusion maps are missing from the provided materials, preventing verification of whether the clinical drop aligns with the imaging trajectory.

The proposed multi-site trial requires a power analysis targeting at least 120 participants per group to detect a moderate effect size with 80% confidence, and must include a False Discovery Rate correction to prevent the small sample from inflating the Type I error rate.

The analysis relies on a fitting algorithm that does not explicitly control for the Gaussian assumption in DTI, raising the methodological concern that the detected Free-Water signal is an artifact of noise absorption rather than a distinct biological change.

The proposed definitive study design must include a priori ROI definitions to eliminate the circularity introduced by post hoc ROI selection, which creates a methodological bias that standard statistical corrections cannot fully repair.

documents: The study utilized data from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) database, including participants with healthy controls (HC) and mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease (AD).
In the Alzheimer's disease (AD) group, the free-water (FW) index was significantly elevated in the corpus callosum and fornix regions compared to healthy controls.

The study included 30 healthy control subjects (17 females, age 73 ± 6) and 28 Alzheimer's disease subjects (15 females, age 75 ± 7). Student t-tests revealed significant differences between the Alzheimer's disease and healthy control cohorts in Mini-Mental State Examination scores (t=-5.21, p<0.0001) and Clinical Dementia Rating scores (t=-8.22, p<0.0001), but not in age (t=-1.51, p=0.137).

The Alzheimer's disease cohort comprised 16 subjects with a Clinical Dementia Rating of 0.5, 10 subjects with a Clinical Dementia Rating of 1, 1 subject with a Clinical Dementia Rating of 2, and 1 subject with a Clinical Dementia Rating of 3, while all 30 healthy control subjects had a Clinical Dementia Rating of 0.

The study included 30 healthy controls (17 females; age 73 ± 6 years) and 28 Alzheimer's disease subjects (15 females; age 75 ± 7 years), with Clinical Dementia Rating scores ranging from 0.5 to 3.0 for the Alzheimer's disease group and 0 for the healthy control group.
The mean Mini-Mental State Examination score was 29.10 (S.D. 1.24) for healthy controls and 24.18 (S.D. 5.02) for Alzheimer's disease subjects.

Diffusion MRI data were acquired on a 3 T Siemens scanner using 64 diffusion-encoding directions with a b-value of 1000 s/mm², TR/TE of 11,000/87.0 ms, flip angle of 90°, matrix of 96×96, field of view of 24.0 × 24.0 cm, slice thickness of 2.5 mm, and 64 axial slices.

Comparisons of DTI-, FW-DTI- metrics, and FW maps between groups were performed using the FSL Randomise tool with threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) and a correction for multiple comparisons via Family-Wise Error (FWE) rate at a 0.01 level.
A white matter mask was defined using a threshold of 0.2 on the average values of fractional anisotropy (FA) from standard DTI and was applied to the other DTI maps.
For each voxel, DTI-derived metrics were fitted by an Analysis of Covariance model (ANCOVA), which included age and sex as covariates, with the number of randomized permutations set at 5,000.
All results are reported with a significance threshold of p value < 0.01, corrected for Family-Wise Error (FWE).
For the cognitively impaired group (AD only), the voxel-based relationship between MMSE scores and DTI metrics was assessed through Randomise with significance at p-value < 0.01 (FWE-corrected).
Student's t-test did not show any difference in age (t = -1.51; p = 0.137) or sex (t = 0.233; p = 0.817) between the healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) groups.
Significant differences were found for MMSE (t = -5.21; p < 0.0001) and for CDR (t = -8.22; p < 0.0001) between the healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) groups.

For standard DTI, substantial overlap was observed for clusters with higher axial diffusivity (AxD) and higher radial diffusivity (RD), including 85% of the cingulum (hippocampus), 76% of the fornix, and 49% of the sagittal stratum.

FW-DTI clusters where Alzheimer's disease (AD) had lower FA_t values than healthy controls (HC) covered 71% of the fornix and 19.2% of the corpus callosum (CC), which are smaller than the standard FA clusters covering 93.3% and 35.5% of these regions, respectively, at p<0.01 FWE corrected.
A small cluster inside the body of the corpus callosum (CC) showed higher radial diffusivity (RD_t) in the Alzheimer's disease (AD) group at p<0.05 FWE corrected.
In FW-DTI analysis, lower FA_t values overlapped with lower axial diffusivity (AxD_t) and radial diffusivity (RD_t) values in 4.8% of the fornix.
Significant differences between groups using the FW index were identified at p<0.01 FWE corrected, with only clusters showing higher FW values in AD compared with HC found.
Table 2 reports brain locations for significant group differences at p<0.01 FWE corrected, except for the RD (HC) < RD (AD) column which is reported at p<0.05 FWE corrected.
For the JHU WM tract atlas, the percent volume of the cluster inside the Left ATR for RD (HC) < RD (AD) under Standard DTI was 31.06%, and for FA (HC) < FA (AD) under Free-water DTI was 7.91%.
For the ICBM-DTI-81 WM atlas, the percent volume of the cluster inside the Genu of CC for FA (HC) > FA (AD) under Standard DTI was 44.91%, and for FA (HC) > FA (AD) under Free-water DTI was 30.35%.
For the ICBM-DTI-81 WM atlas, the percent volume of the cluster inside the Body of CC for RD (HC) < RD (AD) under Standard DTI was 70.68%, and for RD (HC) < RD (AD) under Free-water DTI was 1.21%.
For the ICBM-DTI-81 WM atlas, the percent volume of the cluster inside the Fornix for FA (HC) > FA (AD) under Standard DTI was 93.33%, and for FA (HC) > FA (AD) under Free-water DTI was 70.91%.

The comparison between the Healthy Control (HC) and Alzheimer's Disease (AD) groups showed no significant difference for age or sex (t=0.233; p=0.817), but significant differences were found for the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) (t=-5.21; p<0.0001) and Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) (t=-8.22; p<0.0001).

Standard Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) analysis revealed that the Alzheimer's Disease (AD) group had lower fractional anisotropy (FA) than the Healthy Control (HC) group in a cluster covering 93.3% of the fornix and a cluster covering 35.5% of the corpus callosum (CC).

The Alzheimer's Disease (AD) group exhibited higher fractional anisotropy (FA) values than the Healthy Control (HC) group in the right anterior thalamic radiation (ATR), cortical spinal tract (CST), posterior limb of internal capsule (PLIC), and superior corona radiata (SCR).

All significant clusters for axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) corresponded to higher values in the Alzheimer's Disease (AD) group compared to the Healthy Control (HC) group, with no clusters showing lower AxD or RD values in the AD group.

The significant clusters for fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AxD), and radial diffusivity (RD) were identified using an Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) with a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for Family-Wise Error (FWE).

Figure 2 reports ANCOVA clusters for FA_t, AD_t, and RD_t between HC and AD subjects at a significance threshold of p < 0.01 FWE-corrected, with the exception of RD_t (HC) < RD_t (AD), which is reported at p < 0.05 FWE-corrected.
Figure 3 reports ANCOVA clusters for the FW index between HC and AD subjects at a significance threshold of p < 0.01 FWE-corrected, with no significant clusters found for FW (HC) > FW (AD).
Significant clusters for the FW index between HC and AD covered 34% of the total WM mask, including the fornix, cingulum, and CC.

Significantly higher MA values in AD compared with HC were observed in the right CST, right PLIC, right SCR, and right SFOF, while lower MA values in AD compared with HC were found in the genu of CC and the external capsule.
Clusters of significant differences between groups for the MA index were reported at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for Family Wise Error (FWE).
The percent volume of the cluster inside the Genu of the corpus callosum was 10.07% for standard MA and 6.76% for FW-MA in the HC>AD comparison.
The percent volume of the cluster inside the external capsule was 10.40% for standard MA and 6.26% for FW-MA in the HC>AD comparison.
The percent volume of the cluster inside the right superior corona radiata was 2.34% for standard MA and 2.87% for FW-MA in the HC<AD comparison.
No significant voxel-based correlation was found between the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and either standard or FW-DTI metrics at the p<0.05 FWE corrected level.
For the AD group, the correlation between fractional anisotropy (FA) and axial diffusivity (AxD) increased from 0.160 for standard metrics to 0.856 for FW-corrected metrics.
For the AD group, the correlation between fractional anisotropy (FA) and radial diffusivity (RD) changed from -0.464 for standard metrics to -0.803 for FW-corrected metrics.

Lower fractional anisotropy (FA) and higher mean diffusivity (MD) in the fornix were observed in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and remained significant after free water (FW) correction, indicating true pathological changes rather than partial volume effects.

Large clusters of lower FA were observed in the genu and body of the corpus callosum (CC) in AD using both standard and FW-corrected diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), with minimal splenial changes particularly evident in FW-DTI.

Higher FA was observed in bilateral anterior thalamic radiation (ATR) and corticospinal tracts (CST) in AD compared with healthy controls using FW-DTI, whereas standard DTI showed smaller clusters of higher FA limited to the right hemisphere in the ATR, CST, posterior limb of internal capsule (PLIC), and superior corona radiata (SCR).

Higher mean anisotropy (MA) was found in AD subjects in the right CST, PLIC, and SCR, while lower MA was found in the left ATR, forceps major and minor, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF), uncinate fasciculus (UF), genu of CC, anterior corona radiata, and external capsule.

The study used a voxel-based approach for white matter analysis, noting that the atlases covered 84% of the white matter mask, which is particularly relevant for the fractional anisotropy index that showed widespread changes outside of the atlas regions.
No significant voxel-based correlations (p < 0.01 FWE corrected) were observed between standard DTI and FW-DTI metrics and the MMSE score.

In the AD group, FW volume fraction was higher in the cingulum hippocampal part (85.16%), cingulate gyrus part (56.34%), ILF (52%), IFOF (40%), forceps major (approximately 40%), forceps minor (approximately 40%), ATR (31.39%), fornix (95.6%), and the CC genu, body, and splenium (approximately 56% of total CC).
Approximately 42% of the FW clusters were located in white matter outside the regions specified by the atlases, with FW increases found in several regions bordering various sulcal fundi.
No significant voxel-wise correlations between MMSE and DTI metrics were observed in the AD cohort before or after FW correction.
The reported correlation between DTI free-water metrics and MMSE scores is constrained by a skewed CDR distribution, preventing proof of the relationship across the full disease spectrum.

Verification of the DTI free-water metric's superiority over standard tools is blocked by the absence of the exact diffusion modeling software version and specific parameter settings for free-water estimation.
Independent replication of the DTI free-water fraction maps is impeded by the lack of subject-level raw data and the specific script used to generate these maps.
The study included a sample of 18 participants diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment at baseline and Alzheimer's disease at the 2-year follow-up examination.
Statistical models controlling for age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status identified AxD in the left retrolenticular internal capsule as a significant independent predictor of CDR changes.

AxD changes in the left retrolenticular internal capsule, left posterior corona radiata, left fornix, and right superior longitudinal fasciculus showed significant correlations with cognitive decline, whereas RD changes were not significantly associated with CDR changes in any region.
The final analysis included 18 participants with a mean age of 72.00 ± 8.69 years, of whom 6 (33.33%) were female.
Participants were classified into cognitively normal, MCI, and AD groups based on clinical dementia rating (CDR) scores in accordance with ADNI criteria.
Cognitive decline was defined as the change in CDR scores over a 2-year period, calculated as CDR at follow-up minus CDR at baseline.

The study included 18 participants (age 72.00 ± 8.69; 6 [33.33%] females) diagnosed with MCI at baseline who progressed to AD at follow-up, after excluding 44 participants with missing baseline or follow-up DTI images from an initial pool of 62 MCI-to-AD progressors.
Follow-up assessments for the 18 included participants were conducted at 24.78 ± 1.75 months after the baseline assessment.

The TBSS analysis utilized permutation testing with 5,000 iterations to generate a null distribution of t-values and applied threshold-free cluster enhancement to correct for multiple comparisons at the voxel level with a significance threshold of P < 0.05.
A general linear model incorporated age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status as independent variables to account for confounding factors in the analysis of AxD and RD dependent variables.

The white matter skeleton was constructed using an FA template space derived from 18 participants and refined with a threshold of 0.2 to include only voxels with sufficient fractional anisotropy values.

Region-of-interest analyses for the cingulum, corpus callosum, and uncinate fasciculus were conducted post hoc based on significant whole-brain differences, introducing a threat to validity that requires cautious interpretation of the statistical tests.

The decreased diffusivity metrics (AxD and RD) exhibited no statistically significant differences at P<0.05 after correcting for multiple comparisons (FWE). The color intensity scale in the TBSS results represents statistical significance, with red indicating values closer to P=0.05 and yellow approaching P=0.

The largest voxel sizes for the increase in AxD were observed in the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) and posterior corona radiata (PCR). Widespread increases in AxD and RD were observed in the internal capsule, corona radiata, and cingulum cingulate gyrus during the two-year follow-up period.

Table 2 reports the voxel sizes for significant changes in AxD and RD, with the splenium of the corpus callosum showing 1625 voxels for AxD and 1387 voxels for RD. The body of the corpus callosum exhibited 1073 voxels for AxD and 805 voxels for RD, while the genu of the corpus callosum showed 736 voxels for AxD and 867 voxels for RD.

A general linear model incorporated age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status as independent variables with AxD/RD as the dependent variable, while Spearman's correlation analysis controlled for age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, and baseline CDR score. Uncorrected P-values were reported for the correlation analyses because applying the Bonferroni correction to the small sample size would have significantly lowered statistical power and eliminated significant associations.

A post hoc power analysis was conducted using G*Power version 3.1 to evaluate the adequacy of the sample size in detecting meaningful correlations between clinical progression and changes in white matter integrity. Multiple linear regression analysis evaluated the independent contributions of AxD and RD changes to clinical development, using the change in CDR scores as the dependent variable and AxD and RD as independent variables while treating age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, and baseline CDR score as confounders.

The CDR score showed a statistically significant increase (P<0.001) over 2 years, rising from a mean score of 2.42 ± 1.17 at baseline to 4.64 ± 1.44 at follow-up. No significant differences were found between the included group (n=18) and excluded group (n=44) for age (P=0.909), sex (P=0.578), education level (P=0.967), APOE ε4 carrier status (P=0.251), or baseline CDR (P=0.074).

TBSS analysis revealed a significant increase in Axial Diffusivity (AxD) and Radial Diffusivity (RD) values at follow-up compared to baseline across the corpus callosum, internal capsule, corona radiata, thalamic radiation, lateral temporoparietal regions, longitudinal fasciculus, sagittal and external capsule, cingulate gyrus, fornix, and tapetum.

The study sample consisted of 18 participants (6 females, 12 males) with a mean baseline age of 72.00 years (SD 8.69) and a mean follow-up age of 74.00 years (SD 8.69), showing a significant age change (P < 0.001).
Baseline Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores increased significantly from a mean of 2.42 (SD 1.17) at baseline to 4.64 (SD 1.44) at follow-up (P < 0.001).

The sample included 6 APOE ε4 carriers (33.33%) and 12 non-carriers (66.67%), with education levels distributed as 2 participants (11.11%) with 10-12 years, 7 participants (38.89%) with 13-16 years, and 9 participants (50.00%) with more than 16 years of education.
The association between CDR changes and diffusion metrics exhibited a weak positive trend with a p-value of 0.194, which was not statistically significant.

TBSS analysis revealed significant increases in AxD and RD in the corpus callosum, cingulum, and superior longitudinal fasciculus, while RD changes across all examined white matter regions did not significantly associate with CDR changes.

TBSS analysis revealed significant changes in AxD and RD across the corpus callosum, cingulum, cingulate gyrus, superior longitudinal fasciculus, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, and internal capsule.

Post hoc power analysis using G*Power (version 3.1) indicated the study had 93.7% power to detect a correlation of r=0.704 and 86.3% power for the average observed correlation across all significant regions (mean r=0.644), with alpha=0.05 and N=18.
No significant correlations were observed between the changes in radial diffusivity (RD) and changes in Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores across any of the examined white matter regions.

In multiple linear regression analyses adjusting for age, APOE epsilon 4 status, education, sex, and baseline CDR, axial diffusivity (AxD) changes in the left retrolenticular internal capsule were significantly associated with CDR changes (beta [95% CI] = 0.0141 [0.0005, 0.0277], P=0.044).

AxD changes in the right superior longitudinal fasciculus (beta [95% CI] = 0.0230 [-0.0069, 0.0528], P=0.117), right sagittal stratum (beta [95% CI] = 0.0157 [-0.0068, 0.0382], P=0.152), left superior longitudinal fasciculus (beta [95% CI] = 0.0144 [-0.0074, 0.0361], P=0.172), and left posterior thalamic radiation (beta [95% CI] = 0.0093 [-0.0056, 0.0242], P=0.194) exhibited weak positive trends with CDR changes that were not statistically significant.

Axonal degeneration changes (AxD) in the left retrolenticular region of the internal capsule, left posterior corona radiata, left fornix cres stria terminalis, and right superior longitudinal fasciculus exhibited significant correlations with changes in Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores.

Multivariate regression analysis indicated that axonal degeneration changes (AxD) in the left retrolenticular internal capsule correlated with Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) changes, while AxD increases in the right superior longitudinal fasciculus, right sagittal stratum, left superior longitudinal fasciculus, and left posterior thalamic tract showed minor positive trends with CDR changes that did not exhibit statistical significance.

The study acknowledges that its analyses may have been underpowered and recommends further studies with larger samples to explore whether APOE ε4 status moderates the relationship between DTI metrics and cognitive decline.
The study utilized a sample size of n=18, which limits generalizability and reduces statistical power, increasing the likelihood of overlooking subtle changes.
Uncorrected p-values were reported due to the small sample size, acknowledging a risk of inflated false-positive rates and the need for future validation using False Discovery Rate corrections.
ROI analyses were conducted post hoc based on TBSS findings, raising concerns about circular reasoning that require validation via a priori ROI definitions or independent datasets.
Potential interaction effects between APOE ε4 status and white matter changes were not tested because the limited sample size and small number of ε4 carriers rendered such analyses underpowered.
Correlations between AxD increases in the right SLF, right SS, left SLF, and left PT and CDR changes showed minor positive trends but did not exhibit statistical significance.

The white matter atlases utilized in the Free-Water DTI analysis covered only 84% of total white matter, leaving 16% of the structure unmapped. This coverage gap constitutes a threat to validity, as the reported widespread Free Water changes may be attributable to unaccounted-for noise or partial volume issues in the unmapped regions rather than true pathology.

The study enrolled 43 Alzheimer's disease patients and 16 healthy controls who underwent diffusion spectrum imaging and conventional magnetic resonance imaging. Pearson correlation analysis and receiver operating characteristic analysis were used to assess relationships and diagnostic performance.
Diffusion metrics RTOP, RTAP, ICVF, and FA showed significant correlations with MMSE and MoCA scores, with RTOP and RTAP exhibiting the strongest relationship to cognitive function.

The statistical analysis employed nonparametric permutation tests with 5000 random permutations and used threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) for multiple comparison correction with a statistical threshold of p < 0.001.

Pearson correlation analysis was used to assess the relationship between clinical cognitive scores and diffusion parameter values, with a statistical significance criterion of p < 0.05 and a false discovery rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons.
The diffusion MRI acquisition protocol utilized 24 directions at b=1000 s/mm² and 3 directions at b=3000 s/mm², totaling 128 diffusion samples with a scan time of 10 minutes and 8 seconds.
Raw diffusion imaging data were processed using eddy current correction via FSL and denoised with a Gaussian filter having a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 3 mm.
The Fractional Anisotropy (FA) metric derived from the DTI model represents diffusion asymmetry within a voxel and theoretically ranges between 0 and 1.

The primary analysis enrolled a total of 43 patients with mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease and 16 healthy controls. Of the 43 patients, 25 successfully completed both the Mini-Mental Status Examination and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment.

The diagnostic criteria for mild cognitive impairment required a subjective cognitive complaint plus objective cognitive impairment defined as at least one test Z value less than -1.5, with an activities of daily living scale decrease of less than 20%.

The diagnostic criteria for Alzheimer's disease required progressive episodic memory impairment plus at least one cognitive impairment, defined by a Clinical Dementia Rating score of at least 1 and a Functional Activities Questionnaire score of at least 9.

The inclusion criteria for healthy controls were no evidence of cognitive impairment, a Mini-Mental Status Examination score of at least 25, a Montreal Cognitive Assessment score of at least 25, and a Clinical Dementia Rating score of 0.

The exclusion criteria for all participants were severe cerebrovascular disorder, severe white matter hyperintensity, a history of psychiatric illness or severe injury, use of medications that influence cognition, left-handedness, contraindications to MRI, and poor-quality MRI images due to movement artifacts.

The diffusion spectrum imaging sequence was acquired on a 3.0T MRI scanner with a repetition time of 4400 ms, echo time of 108 ms, field of view of 220 x 220 mm^2, slice thickness of 2.0 mm, and voxel size of 2.0 x 2.0 x 2.0 mm^2.

The diffusion spectrum imaging acquisition included a total of 128 diffusion sampling directions across b-values ranging from 0 to 3000 s/mm^2, with a total scan time of approximately 10 minutes and 8 seconds.

The study included 43 Alzheimer's disease patients and 16 healthy controls, with significant group differences in age (P=0.005), education (P=0.009), MMSE scores (P<0.001), and MoCA scores (P<0.001), while gender distribution showed no significant difference (P=0.770).

Diffusion parameter maps identified regions with significant statistical values at P<0.001, where red indicated increased parameter values and blue indicated decreased parameter values in the Alzheimer's disease group compared to the healthy control group.
In the Alzheimer's disease group, ISOVF values were significantly increased in the body of corpus callosum, splenium of corpus callosum, external capsule, and cerebral peduncle (p<0.001).

MAP-MRI parameters MSD and QIV were significantly higher in the frontal lobe, occipital parietal lobe, cerebral peduncle, and corpus callosum in the Alzheimer's disease group compared to the healthy control group (p<0.001).

MAP-MRI parameters NGRad, RTAP, RTOP, and RTPP were significantly lower in the genu of corpus callosum, body of corpus callosum, splenium of corpus callosum, anterior corona radiata R/L, and superior corona radiata R/L in the Alzheimer's disease group compared to the healthy control group (p<0.001).
MAP-MRI parameters NG and NGAx were significantly decreased in the anterior corona radiata R/L in the Alzheimer's disease group compared to the healthy control group (p<0.001).
The statistical analysis used a significance level of p<0.05 and a false discovery rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons.

Regression models between diffusion parameters and Alzheimer's disease were constructed using multivariate binary logistic regression analysis adjusted for the square of age, gender, and years of education.

The diagnostic performance of diffusion parameter values in distinguishing Alzheimer's disease was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC) analysis to calculate sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and area under the curve (AUC).
The study included a sample size of 43 Alzheimer's disease patients and 16 healthy volunteers.

The average age in the Alzheimer's disease group was significantly higher than in the healthy control group (p=0.005), while years of education (p=0.009), MMSE scores (p<0.001), and MoCA scores (p<0.001) were significantly lower in the Alzheimer's disease group.
There was no significant difference in gender between the Alzheimer's disease group and the healthy control group.

In the DTI model, the Alzheimer's disease group exhibited significantly higher AxD, MD, and RD values in the body of the corpus callosum, splenium of the corpus callosum, and anterior corona radiata R/L compared with the healthy control group (p<0.001).

In the DTI model, the Alzheimer's disease group exhibited notably decreased FA values in the middle cerebellar peduncle, genu of corpus callosum, body of corpus callosum, splenium of corpus callosum, anterior corona radiata R/L, and superior longitudinal fasciculus R/L compared with the healthy control group (p<0.001).

In the NODDI model, the Alzheimer's disease group exhibited significantly higher ECVF values in the genu of corpus callosum, body of corpus callosum, splenium of corpus callosum, and anterior corona radiata R/L.

Anterior corona radiata R/L values were significantly decreased in the AD group compared with the HC group (p<0.001). Correlation analyses were performed in 25 AD patients between DTI, NODDI, and MAP-MRI parameters and MMSE and MoCA scores.

FA values in the fornix (r=0.740, p<0.001), anterior corona radiata L (r=0.617, p<0.001), and stria terminalis R (r=0.715, p<0.001) exhibited strong correlations with MMSE scores. FA values in the fornix (r=0.690, p<0.001), stria terminalis R (r=0.644, p<0.001), and stria terminalis L (r=0.617, p<0.001) demonstrated strong correlations with MoCA scores.

ECVF values in the anterior corona radiata R (r=0.642, p<0.001), ICVF values in the splenium of corpus callosum (r=0.666, p<0.001), and ISOVF values in the stria terminalis R (r=0.604, p<0.001) exhibited the strongest correlations with MMSE scores among NODDI-derived parameters.

The intracellular volume fraction (ICVF) values in the splenium of the corpus callosum showed the strongest correlation with Montreal cognitive assessment (MoCA) scores (r=0.649, p<0.001). No extracellular volume fraction (ECVF), orientation dispersion index (ODI), or isotropic volume fraction (ISOVF) values for any fiber were significantly correlated with MoCA scores.

Return-to-axis probability (RTAP) values in the right stria terminalis (r=0.737, p<0.001) and return-to-origin probability (RTOP) values in the right stria terminalis (r=0.734, p<0.001) exhibited the strongest correlation with Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores. RTAP values in the right stria terminalis (r=0.699, p<0.001) and RTOP values in the right cerebral peduncle (r=0.717, p<0.001) exhibited the strongest correlation with MoCA scores.

Diffusion tensor imaging radial diffusivity (DTI-RD) demonstrated the best diagnostic performance for Alzheimer's disease or mild cognitive impairment in the splenium of the corpus callosum (p=0.021, AUC=0.86, 95% CI 0.76-0.95), fornix (p=0.002, AUC=0.93, 95% CI 0.86-1.00), right cerebral peduncle (p=0.002, AUC=0.95, 95% CI 0.91-1.00), left cerebral peduncle (p=0.021, AUC=0.88, 95% CI 0.79-0.97), and right stria terminalis (p=0.004, AUC=0.92, 95% CI 0.84-0.99).
Diffusion tensor imaging mean diffusivity (DTI-MD) demonstrated the best diagnostic performance in the right anterior corona radiata (p=0.005, AUC=0.92).

The NG, NGAx, and NGRad values of the genu of the corpus callosum, splenium of the corpus callosum, anterior corona radiata, and superior corona radiata were lower in the AD group compared with the HC group. The RTAP, RTOP, and RTPP values of the corpus callosum, corona radiata, fornix, and cerebral peduncle were decreased in the AD group.

The MSD and QIV values of the frontal lobe, parietal lobe, temporal lobe, cerebral peduncles, and corpus callosum were substantially higher in the AD group. Patients with AD showed higher ECVF and ISOVF values, as well as lower ICVF values, compared with HCs.

No significant difference in the ODI values was observed between the HC and AD groups at the significant threshold. The lack of significance in ODI may arise from inherent limitations of the Watson distribution used in NODDI modeling, including reduced accuracy in regions with kissing fibers, crossing axons, and diffuse pathological changes.

A reduction in the dendrite density was observed in the temporal lobe and hippocampus of AD patients through the NODDI model, which was consistent with the decreased FA values reported in the DTI study. MAP detected more extensive microstructural changes across brain regions compared with NODDI.
ROC analysis showed no significant statistical difference in AUC between DTI-derived RD/MD and NODDI-derived ISOVF/ECVF parameters after DeLong's test.
DeLong's test provided robust statistical support for the superiority of MAP-derived RTOP over NODDI-derived ECVF in the right anterior corona radiata.
MAP-MRI parameters outperformed NODDI and DTI parameters in their association with cognitive function, with RTOP and RTAP exhibiting the most robust correlations with MMSE and MoCA scores.

The study lacked positron emission tomography (PET) examinations or pathologic verification confirming tau protein deposition in participants with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI).
The AD groups were not divided into various subtypes due to the relatively small sample size, limiting the wide applicability of the results.

The analysis did not consider the presence of white matter hyperintensities (WMH), and since diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) parameters are associated with WMH in individuals older than 60 years, the results may have been influenced by heterogeneous macrostructural white matter impairments.

The Free-Water DTI pipeline is non-reproducible because the specific FSL EDIFY software version and exact thresholding values are not provided, leaving the processing configuration as an opaque black box.

The Free-Water DTI study ignores white matter hyperintensities, a macrostructural confound that threatens validity by potentially explaining the observed cognitive decline rather than demonstrating the superiority of the Free-Water metric.

Across the three Free-Water DTI papers, the reported effects are statistically significant but lack 95% confidence intervals, resulting in wide effect size intervals that prevent distinguishing true biological signals from noise given the low statistical power.

The methodological flaw of defining regions of interest based on initial findings creates a circularity that no statistical correction can fully repair, rendering the claim of specific anatomical localization speculative until independent, a priori regions are validated.
Verification of the circularity claim requires the exact coordinate files for the a priori regions of interest and the raw TBSS output maps to compare them directly against the post hoc regions.

Independent verification of the tractography analysis is blocked by the absence of specific mask files, thresholding parameters for the initial whole-brain scan, and the version of the tractography software used.

The absence of multiple comparison correction on Free-Water metrics leaves the family-wise error rate uncontrolled, and the failure to adjust for white matter hyperintensities renders the reported effect size indistinguishable from macrostructural noise.

The exclusion of 44 participants introduces a selection bias that serves as a plausible alternative explanation for the observed Free-Water effects, suggesting the signals may reflect technical artifacts rather than specific biological pathology.

The use of post hoc ROI selection introduces circularity, meaning any replication attempt re-executes the specific methodological errors of the original Free-Water DTI analysis rather than testing a new hypothesis. This design flaw limits the study to hypothesis generation, as the clinical specificity of the Free-Water signal cannot be validated without a priori definitions.

The claim that the new imaging signal detects early disruptions missed by standard DTI lacks validity due to the absence of a priori validation, a proper control group, and independent replication, leaving the possibility of algorithmic overfitting to noise in a small sample unaddressed.

The proposed multi-site trial requires a power analysis targeting n = 120 per group to achieve 80% power for detecting a moderate effect size, alongside a False Discovery Rate correction to control the Type I error rate and prevent the Free-Water signal from being indistinguishable from noise.

The Free-Water correction's utility is limited by the lack of independent validation and a priori region-of-interest definitions, meaning the tool remains hypothesis-generating rather than a confirmed diagnostic for individuals with early memory complaints.
