documents: A more detailed brain scan method provides a clearer and more accurate picture of brain tissue damage in people with Alzheimer's disease than the standard method. The study confirms that this improved scan is better at showing the specific areas of the brain that are affected by the condition.

Scans of the brain's white matter can show signs of damage before memory loss or other symptoms of Alzheimer's disease appear, but these early signs are not always clearly linked to how well a person is thinking.

The study compared thirty healthy older adults with twenty-eight people diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease, finding that the people with Alzheimer's had significantly lower scores on tests of memory and daily function.

Standard brain scans can be misleading in Alzheimer's disease because fluid buildup from dying brain cells mixes with the tissue signals, so a new method was used to remove this extra fluid to get a clearer picture of the actual brain tissue.

The study found no clear link between the brain scan measurements and the results of the memory test, meaning these specific scan details did not predict how well people performed on the memory check.
The analysis showed that the brain scan measurements were not related to the score on the memory test, so the scans did not show a connection to how well the participants remembered information.

The evidence is highly confident that specific brain connections show stronger signals in people with Alzheimer's disease than in healthy people, but this finding only shows where the differences are located and does not explain why they occur.

The study found that the brain connections in people with Alzheimer's disease had stronger signals than those in healthy people, and this result was consistent across two different measurement methods.

The analysis identified specific areas in the brain where the signals were stronger in people with Alzheimer's disease compared to healthy people, but it did not find any areas where the signals were weaker in the Alzheimer's group.

The study found that a specific adjustment to brain scan measurements made the results for people with Alzheimer's disease match known patterns of brain damage more closely than the standard measurements did. This suggests the adjusted method provides a more accurate picture of the disease's effects on the brain's white matter.

The evidence indicates that standard brain scan measurements can be less accurate because they are influenced by fluid in the brain, which can obscure the true state of the tissue. The study does not show that this new adjustment method is perfect, but it demonstrates that it improves the reliability of the findings compared to the older method.

The study found that people with early to mild Alzheimer's disease have areas of the brain's wiring where the structure is less healthy, particularly in regions connecting memory and thinking centers. The evidence suggests that the brain tissue in these specific areas is breaking down, but the study did not find a clear link between these physical changes and how well people performed on standard memory tests.

The research indicates that the measured damage to the brain's communication pathways is more reliable when using a newer method that accounts for fluid in the tissue. This improved measurement helps explain why previous studies gave mixed results about how brain structure relates to thinking skills, but it does not prove that these physical changes directly cause memory loss in every person.
A more accurate way of measuring brain tissue structure is needed to better understand how the brain changes in people with Alzheimer's disease, as current methods may miss subtle differences.
The study found that overall memory scores did not match the specific brain changes seen in the scans, suggesting that the relationship between brain damage and memory loss is not simple or direct.
Future research should look at people in the early stages of memory decline or those at high risk for Alzheimer's disease to help identify the condition earlier.
A new method for correcting brain scan data provides a clearer and more reliable picture of the brain damage associated with Alzheimer's disease than standard scanning techniques.
The improved scanning method better captures the specific patterns of brain tissue loss expected in Alzheimer's disease, offering a more precise view of how the condition affects the brain.

Changes in the way brain tissue fibers stretch and spread out were linked to worsening memory and thinking skills in people moving from early memory problems to Alzheimer's disease. The evidence suggests these specific changes can help predict how quickly a person's condition will worsen, but the study did not find a clear link between how much the fibers spread out and the decline in thinking skills.
The study suggests that a specific measure of brain tissue health could be a useful tool for spotting Alzheimer's disease early and tracking how it gets worse over time.
It is not yet known if damage to the brain's communication pathways is one of the very first signs of Alzheimer's disease.
Standard brain scans are not good at spotting subtle damage in the early stages of Alzheimer's disease when the brain has not yet shrunk much.
A specialized type of brain scan can detect subtle changes in the brain's internal structure that standard scans miss, helping to identify early signs of nerve damage.

Brain changes that happen early and get worse over time have been seen in people with mild memory problems who later develop Alzheimer's disease. This gradual worsening highlights the need to spot these changes early and act quickly, especially to understand how small structural shifts in the brain connect to a loss of thinking skills over time.

Most past studies could not capture how brain changes evolve over time because they only looked at a single point in time. Studies that track these changes over a longer period can help explain how brain damage progresses and whether it causes a loss of thinking skills.
Tracking brain changes over time can provide insight into the disease features of Alzheimer's and help determine if brain damage can serve as an early warning sign of the condition.

The study assumed that damage to the brain's white matter, which involves the breakdown of nerve fibers and their protective coating, represents early changes during the shift from mild memory problems to Alzheimer's disease. The study also assumed that this damage is linked to a decline in thinking skills.
The study found that people in the group experienced a large drop in their mental abilities over a two-year period, showing a clear worsening of their condition.

The researchers checked whether the people who were left out of the study because of missing data were different from those who were included, and found no major differences in their age, gender, education, or starting health status.

The study used a specific computer method to align brain scan data from different people, which helps ensure accurate comparisons but may miss early signs of damage in the outer edges of the brain's wiring.

Researchers looked at specific brain areas that showed changes in the overall scan results, so these detailed findings should be viewed as exploratory rather than definitive proof of specific problems.
The analysis accounted for factors like age, sex, education, and a specific genetic trait to better understand the changes in the brain's structure over time.

The study found no evidence that age, sex, education level, or the presence of a specific gene variant affected the results. The confidence in these specific comparisons is low because the differences were not statistically significant.

The study showed that the physical structure of the brain's connection pathways changed significantly between the first and second examination. This indicates a measurable shift in the health of these neural connections over time for the people involved.

The participants in the study were older at the second examination than at the first, and their overall level of dementia was higher at the second examination. The evidence strongly supports that these changes occurred over the study period.

Changes in the health of the left retrolenticular part of the internal capsule were linked to changes in clinical dementia ratings, but this link was not strong enough to be considered a definite finding. The study did not find a clear connection between changes in the radial diffusivity of white matter and changes in clinical dementia ratings.

Damage to specific white matter pathways in the brain is linked to worsening cognitive decline in people with dementia. The evidence is moderately strong for connections in the left internal capsule, left posterior corona radiata, left fornix, and right superior longitudinal fasciculus, but the study does not show that these changes happen in every person or in other brain regions.

The study found that changes in one type of brain tissue measurement were linked to worsening memory and thinking skills, but another type of measurement showed no such link. The evidence is not strong enough to prove a direct cause-and-effect relationship.

Damage to the main bridge connecting the two halves of the brain can weaken memory, attention, and language skills. Damage to other specific brain pathways can also lead to difficulties with walking, balance, and complex thinking.

Previous research suggests that as Alzheimer's disease progresses, the structure of the brain's connecting tissues changes. These structural changes are often seen in people with lower scores on memory tests.

Damage to the nerve fibers in specific areas of the brain is linked to worsening memory and thinking skills in people with Alzheimer's disease. This suggests that the loss of these fibers contributes to the decline in a person's ability to function.

The study found that the loss of nerve fibers, rather than the damage to their protective coating, is the main factor causing cognitive decline in the early stages of Alzheimer's disease. This indicates that the early symptoms are driven by the physical breakdown of the nerve connections themselves.

Measurements of nerve fiber damage in the left side of the brain were linked to worsening symptoms, while measurements on the right side showed only a weak and unproven connection. This suggests that the left side of the brain is more strongly affected by the disease progression in terms of cognitive decline.

Damage to the nerve fibers in the brain, rather than the protective coating around them, is the main factor linked to worsening memory and thinking skills in people with Alzheimer's disease. This suggests that monitoring this specific type of nerve damage could help doctors spot the early stages of the disease and track how it is progressing.

Tracking changes in nerve fiber damage over time provides a clearer picture of how the disease develops and affects thinking skills compared to taking a single snapshot. However, this method is not yet ready for routine use in clinics because the measurements are not consistent across different hospitals and there are no standard levels defined to indicate when the damage becomes pathological.

The study's results are not certain because it only included a very small number of people, which makes it hard to know if the findings apply to the wider population. Additionally, the study only used a general severity scale to measure thinking skills, so it did not look at specific abilities like memory or attention, and the measurements themselves may be affected by other factors like inflammation, making it unclear exactly what the changes represent.

The study found that changes in the brain's white matter structure are linked to worsening memory and thinking skills in people moving from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease. However, the researchers noted that the group of people studied may have been too small to fully determine if a specific genetic factor influences this relationship.

A specific measure of brain damage was found to be a sensitive indicator of early disease changes and could help detect and monitor the progression of Alzheimer's disease. The study did not show that this measure is the only factor involved, as other types of brain changes were also observed in fewer areas.

Alzheimer's disease causes a steady decline in memory and thinking skills that eventually leads to a complete loss of independence. The physical damage to brain cells and their connections happens before the brain shrinks in size, making it essential to find ways to detect this early damage.

A common brain scan technique used to study Alzheimer's disease has a built-in limitation that makes it less effective at detecting complex changes in brain tissue. A newer scanning method is increasingly used because it can better identify the specific physical changes in the brain associated with the disease.

People with Alzheimer's disease had higher average ages and lower scores on memory and thinking tests compared to healthy people. The study did not find any difference in the number of men and women between the two groups.

Brain scans showed that people with Alzheimer's disease had changes in specific brain pathways, including the main bridge connecting the two sides of the brain and areas controlling movement. These changes suggest damage to the structure of these nerve connections compared to healthy people.

Measurements of how well nerve fibers are organized in the brain's connection bundle and the right side of the terminal stria are strongly linked to how well a person performs on a basic mental status test. The evidence for this link is very strong.

Measurements of how well nerve fibers are organized in the brain's connection bundle and both sides of the terminal stria are strongly linked to how well a person performs on a detailed cognitive assessment. The evidence for this link is very strong.
This research aims to understand the specific patterns of damage in the brain's white matter associated with Alzheimer's disease and how this damage connects to a decline in thinking skills.

The study seeks to identify which specific measures of brain tissue structure are most useful for detecting Alzheimer's disease and how well these measures correlate with a person's cognitive test scores.
Using a single scanning method to gather data for multiple brain structure models saves time and money while allowing researchers to compare different ways of looking at the brain's internal details.

Advanced brain imaging techniques show that damage to the brain's connecting fibers in people with Alzheimer's disease is more widespread than previously thought, which may help explain how the disease affects thinking and memory.
These imaging methods are considered practical tools for detecting subtle changes in brain tissue that are linked to a person's level of cognitive function.

In people with Alzheimer's disease, the amount of fluid inside the nerve cells in the back part of the brain's central connection was strongly linked to how well they performed on memory and thinking tests. This finding suggests that changes in this specific brain area are a reliable sign of the disease's impact on daily cognitive function.

Measuring the direction of nerve fibers in the brain's emotional and memory pathways showed a strong connection to how well people with Alzheimer's disease scored on mental status exams. This indicates that the health of these specific brain connections is closely tied to the severity of the patient's cognitive decline.

A specific measure of how easily water moves sideways through the brain's main connection bundle was the best single test for distinguishing people with Alzheimer's disease from those with mild memory loss. This means that this particular brain scan feature can help doctors identify the disease earlier and more accurately than other measures in that region.

The evidence indicates that brain changes in people with Alzheimer's disease are more widespread than previously thought, affecting areas involved in memory and executive function as well as the brain stem and cerebellum. This suggests that understanding these broader changes could help explain how the disease causes dementia.

The findings show a clear link between specific types of brain tissue damage and lower scores on cognitive tests, indicating that the decline in thinking abilities is associated with physical changes in the brain. The evidence is strong enough to suggest that measuring these specific tissue changes is a sensitive way to detect the underlying pathology.

The study found that one specific type of brain scan measurement was better at distinguishing between people with Alzheimer's disease and those without it in certain brain regions compared to another measurement. However, the other measurement still provided useful information about the structure of brain tissue, even though it was not as effective at making the distinction on its own.

The study found that brain scans can show changes in the tiny structures of the brain in people with Alzheimer's disease, but the evidence is not certain because the researchers did not use other tests to confirm the specific protein buildup or examine the different types of the disease.
The results might be affected by common white matter changes seen in older adults, which means the findings may not apply to everyone with Alzheimer's disease.

The study concludes that three different types of brain scans are useful for looking at tiny brain changes in Alzheimer's disease, but more research is needed to confirm these methods work well for a wider group of people.

Newer brain scanning methods appear to be useful for finding tiny structural changes in the brain that are linked to memory loss and thinking problems. The evidence suggests these scans can show how severe a person's symptoms are, but they do not prove a specific cause for the damage.

Scans of people with memory loss showed signs of damaged nerve fibers and a loss of the protective coating around them, which suggests the brain tissue is breaking down. These findings indicate the scans are sensitive to the physical changes in the brain that happen as the disease progresses.

Brain scans showed that people with memory loss have more space between their nerve cells and less space inside the cells, likely because protein buildup is squeezing the tissue. This physical crowding disrupts how water moves through the brain, which is what the scans detect.

One specific measure of how nerve fibers bend and spread out did not show a clear difference between people with memory loss and healthy people. This lack of a clear difference might be because the measurement is less accurate in complex areas of the brain where different types of damage happen at the same time.

Standard brain scans were still able to find widespread damage in the white matter of people with memory loss, even though the method has known limits. This shows that standard scans are still valuable for spotting the physical changes in the brain associated with the disease.

A more advanced scanning method found damage in more parts of the brain than a different, simpler method did. This suggests the advanced method is better at picking up the complex, detailed changes in the brain tissue that happen as the disease worsens.

Using different types of brain scans together helps provide a fuller picture of what is happening in the brain. Each scan type captures a different aspect of the disease, so combining them gives a better understanding of how the brain is being affected.
There is a real risk that a test might show a problem that is not actually there, which could cause unnecessary stress, so this scan should not be treated as a final answer for diagnosis.

The method used to measure water in the brain is currently only a way to generate new ideas for research, not a confirmed way to diagnose specific conditions, because we lack independent proof that the signals are real.

Without a very large, carefully controlled study that rules out mathematical errors in the data processing, we cannot be confident that the early warning signs detected by the new scan method are real biological changes rather than just noise.

documents: The study data were obtained from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) database and included both healthy controls and mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease participants.

The study included 30 healthy control subjects (17 females, mean age 73) and 28 Alzheimer's disease subjects (15 females, mean age 75), with MMSE scores of 29.10 (SD 1.24) for healthy controls and 24.18 (SD 5.02) for Alzheimer's disease subjects.
The Alzheimer's disease cohort comprised 16 subjects with CDR 0.5, 10 with CDR 1, 1 with CDR 2, and 1 with CDR 3, while all 30 healthy control subjects had a CDR of 0.

Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics include fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AxD), and radial diffusivity (RD), where FA is calculated from faster diffusivity along fibers and lower perpendicular diffusivity.
A free water (FW) correction algorithm is used to quantify and remove the contribution of extracellular free water to diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics to mitigate partial volume effects.

The study compared fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AxD), radial diffusivity (RD), and mean anisotropy (MA) derived from standard DTI and FW-DTI between Alzheimer's disease (AD) and healthy control (HC) subjects using data from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) brain project.
The analysis included the FW index for both AD and HC groups and voxel-based correlations between all DTI-derived metrics and the mini-mental state examination (MMSE) score.

FW-corrected maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script which is available upon request. The Free Water (FW) model fitting uses a b-value of 1000 s/mm² and sets the diffusion coefficient D_water to 3 × 10⁻³ mm²/s.

The FW model fitting uses a b-value of 1000 s/mm² and sets the diffusion coefficient D_water to 3 × 10⁻³ mm²/s. Standard DTI metrics are reported as AxD, RD, and FA, while FW-corrected DTI metrics are reported as AxD_t, RD_t, and FA_t.

The mode of anisotropy (MA) is calculated using the DTI eigenvalues λ1, λ2, and λ3 with the specific formula provided in the text. MA is mathematically orthogonal to FA and relates to the skewness of the DTI eigenvalues.
The significant clusters in the DTI analysis were reported at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for Family Wise Error (FWE).
The significant cluster sizes for each brain region are reported as a percentage of volume in Table 2.
The study data were downloaded from the OASIS-3 brain project (http://oasis-brains.org/), a freely available neuroimaging dataset for normal aging and Alzheimer's disease.

Inclusion criteria required participants aged 60 to 90 years with 3 T dMRI data available with more than 30 directions, while exclusion criteria removed cognitively impaired participants with non-AD dementia, healthy controls with significant comorbidities, and participants without available MMSE scores.

The study cohort included 30 healthy controls (17 females; mean age 73 years, S.D. 6) and 28 Alzheimer's disease subjects (15 females; mean age 75 years, S.D. 7), with Clinical Dementia Rating scores of zero for all healthy controls and between 0.5 and 3.0 for the Alzheimer's disease group.

All diffusion MRI data were acquired on a 3 T Siemens scanner using 64 diffusion-encoding directions with a b value of 1000 s/mm², TR/TE of 11,000/87.0 ms, a flip angle of 90°, a 96×96 matrix, a 24.0 × 24.0 cm field of view, 2.5 mm slice thickness, and 64 axial slices, alongside one non-diffusion-weighted B0 image.

Preprocessing of the NIFTI format dMRI data was performed using the FMRIB software library (FSL) version 5.0.4 for eddy current and motion correction, and the Brain Extraction Toolbox (BET) for defining brain masks on single B0 images.

DTI standard and FW-corrected maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script that is available upon request, with gradient orientations compensated for rotational registration components prior to B-matrix calculation.

B0 group-wise template images were normalized to the IIT_mean_b0 image using the ANTs symmetric image normalization (SyN) algorithm. Warp fields from the normalization and template creation were used to transfer all DTI maps to the Illinois Institute of Technology (IIT) Human Brain Atlas version 4.1 in International Consortium for Brain Mapping (ICBM)-152 space.
All DTI maps in standard space were smoothed using FSL with an isotropic Gaussian kernel with a sigma of 3 mm.

Comparisons of DTI-, FW-DTI- metrics, and FW maps between groups were performed using the FSL Randomise tool with threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) and a Family-Wise Error (FWE) correction at a 0.01 level. A white matter mask was defined using a threshold of 0.2 on the average values of fractional anisotropy (FA) from standard DTI and applied to other DTI maps.

For each voxel, DTI-derived metrics were fitted by an Analysis of Covariance model (ANCOVA) that included age and sex as covariates. The number of randomized permutations for the statistical analysis was set at 5,000.

Statistically different clusters were labeled according to the Johns Hopkins University (JHU) DTI-based white-matter atlases. All results were reported with a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01, corrected for FWE, except where otherwise noted.

For the cognitively impaired group (AD only), the voxel-based relationship between Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores and DTI metrics was assessed through FSL Randomise with significance at p-value < 0.01 (FWE-corrected).
Supplementary Table 2 reports the mean standard DTI values inside each significant cluster for regions with higher and lower values for each group.
The FW-DTI metric clusters are displayed in Figure 2 panels (a), (b), and (c) for FA_t, AxD_t, and RD_t respectively, with a significance threshold of p<0.01 FWE corrected.
Table 2 reports the significant cluster sizes as percent volume for each brain region.
Supplementary Table 3 shows the mean FW-DTI values inside each significant cluster for regions with higher and lower values for each group.

The ICBM-DTI-81 white-matter atlas defines specific anatomical regions including the corpus callosum (CC), limb of internal capsule (LIC), internal capsule (IC), corona radiate (CR), sagittal stratum (SS), and superior fronto-occipital fasciculus (SFOF).

The ANCOVA analysis for FA_t and AxD_t metrics between HC and AD subjects uses a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for FWE, while the RD_t analysis uses a threshold of p-value < 0.05 FWE-corrected.
The ANCOVA analysis for the FW index between HC and AD subjects uses a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for FWE.
The group-wise significant clusters for the FW index between HC and AD are listed in Table 3.
The group-wise significant clusters for the MA index between HC and AD are listed in Table 4.
Significant differences between groups were identified at p<0.01 FWE corrected, except for the RD (HC) < RD (AD) comparison in the final column which was reported at p<0.05 FWE corrected.

The JHU white-matter tractography atlas abbreviations are ATR (anterior thalamic radiation), CST (cortical spinal tract), CGC (cingulum cingulate gyrus part), CGH (cingulum hippocampal part), IFOF (inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus), ILF (inferior longitudinal fasciculus), and UF (uncinate fasciculus).

The ICBM-DTI-81 white-matter atlas abbreviations are CC (corpus callosum), LIC (limb of internal capsule), IC (internal capsule), CR (corona radiate), SS (sagittal stratum), and SFOF (superior fronto-occipital fasciculus).
The percentage columns in the table indicate the percent volume of the cluster located inside the corresponding brain area.

The study reports group-wise significant clusters for mean anisotropy (MA) using both standard DTI and FW-DTI analysis, with results presented in Table 4 and Figure 4. Figure 4 displays the ANCOVA analysis between healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) subjects for the MA index at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for family-wise error (FWE).

Table 3 lists brain locations for significant differences between groups in FW maps analysis at p < 0.01 (FWE corrected), where the '%' column indicates the percent volume of the cluster inside the corresponding brain area. Only clusters with higher FW values in AD than HC were observed in this table.

The JHU white matter tractography atlas abbreviations are defined as: ATR (anterior thalamic radiation), CST (cortical spinal tract), CGC (cingulum cingulate gyrus part), CGH (cingulum hippocampal part), IFOF (inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus), ILF (inferior longitudinal fasciculus), SLF (superior longitudinal fasciculus), and UF (uncinate fasciculus). The ICBM-DTI-81 white matter atlas abbreviations are defined as: CC (corpus callosum), CP (cerebral peduncle), LIC (limb of internal capsule), IC (internal capsule), CR (corona radiata), SS (sagittal stratum), and EC (external capsule).

The study incorporated a free-water component into the conventional diffusion modeling pipeline to remove free-water-contaminated voxels and produce free-water-corrected DTI metrics and a complementary free-water index.
The study assessed white matter integrity in patients with Alzheimer's disease using both standard and free-water-corrected DTI metrics to mitigate partial volume effects.

The white matter atlases used in the study covered 84% of the white matter mask, which limits the representation of white matter regions, particularly for the Free Water index that showed widespread changes outside of these atlas regions.

The study utilized a voxel-based approach for white matter analysis rather than a skeletonized approach like Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS), and voxel-based correlations between standard DTI and Free Water-DTI metrics and the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score were not significant at p<0.01 Family-Wise Error corrected.
The MA index analysis identified significant clusters at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for Family Wise Error (FWE).
The percent volume of significant clusters for the Right CST was 0.52% for Standard MA (HC<AD) and 0.76% for FW-MA (HC<AD).
The percent volume of significant clusters for the Genu of CC was 10.07% for Standard MA (HC>AD) and 6.76% for FW-MA (HC>AD).
The percent volume of significant clusters for the EC was 10.40% for Standard MA (HC>AD) and 6.26% for FW-MA (HC>AD).

The JHU white-matter tractography atlas abbreviations used are ATR (anterior thalamic radiation), CST (cortical spinal tract), IFOF (inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus), ILF (inferior longitudinal fasciculus), and UF (uncinate fasciculus).
No significant voxel-based correlation was found between MMSE and either standard or FW-DTI metrics at p<0.05 FWE corrected level.
For the AD group, the correlation between FA and AxD increased from 0.160 (standard) to 0.856 (FW-corrected).
For the AD group, the correlation between FA and RD increased from -0.464 (standard) to -0.803 (FW-corrected).

The fornix is identified as a region particularly prone to partial volume effects (PVEs) due to its proximity to the lateral ventricles, a factor that may be exacerbated by atrophy-related ventricular expansion in Alzheimer's Disease.

The study notes that standard FA decreases in the fornix and corpus callosum remained after Free Water (FW) correction, indicating these metrics reflect true pathological changes rather than artifacts.
In the corpus callosum, large clusters of lower FA were observed in the genu and body with minimal splenial changes, particularly when using Free Water-DTI (FW-DTI) metrics.

The corpus callosum is described as having a substantial Free Water (FW) component, suggesting that the inclusion of FW correction algorithms could improve the accuracy of DTI metrics in the presence of neurodegenerative changes.

Higher FA values in Alzheimer's Disease compared with healthy controls were observed in bilateral anterior thalamic radiation (ATR) and corticospinal tract (CST), as well as internal capsule and corona radiata, using Free Water-DTI (FW-DTI).

Using standard DTI, smaller clusters of higher FA were observed in the right hemisphere (versus bilateral for FW-DTI) in the ATR, CST, posterior limb of the internal capsule (PLIC), and superior corona radiata (SCR).

Mean Anisotropy (MA) was higher in Alzheimer's Disease subjects in the right CST, PLIC, and SCR, while lower MA was found in the left ATR, forceps major and minor, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF), uncinate fasciculus (UF), genu of the corpus callosum, anterior corona radiata, and external capsule.

The text identifies a major drawback of standard DTI methods as the inability to resolve different fiber orientations within a voxel, which arises from the assumption of Gaussian diffusion implicit in the tensor model.
The OASIS brain database provides longitudinal MRI data for nondemented and demented older adults, as described by Marcus et al. (2010) and Ardekani et al. (2014).
The FSL software suite implements functional and structural MR image analysis, including the fast robust automated brain extraction algorithm by Smith (2002).
Andersson and Sotiropoulos (2016) describe an integrated approach to correction for off-resonance effects and subject movement in diffusion MR imaging.
The Mini-mental state examination (MMSE) is a practical method for grading the cognitive state of patients, as described by Folstein et al. (1975).
The data for the study was provided by the OASIS project, which was supported by NIH Grants P50 AG05681, P01 AG03991, R01 AG021910, P50 MH071616, U24 RR021382, and R01 MH56584.
Supplementary material for the study is available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-86505-7.
The study utilized a 3T scanner with 1.5mm isotropic resolution, but the slice timing parameter was not specified, which is a critical gap for replicating the BOLD signal preprocessing pipeline.

The exact software version for the water quantification pipeline and the raw data availability statement are missing, which blocks the reproduction of the specific water-type imaging metric used to spot Alzheimer's damage.

The specific preprocessing parameters for the water-type imaging metric are absent from the text, preventing verification of whether standard tools yield the same results as the study's implementation.
All relevant data for the study are contained within the manuscript and its Supporting Information files.

The study selected eighteen participants diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) at baseline and Alzheimer's disease (AD) at follow-up from the AD Neuroimaging Initiative for a 2-year longitudinal analysis.
Statistical models for the tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) analysis controlled for age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status.

The study used data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database (adni.loni.usc.edu) accessed on 14 February 2024, including participants with Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI), cognitive assessments, and demographic evaluations at baseline and a 2-year follow-up.

The final analysis included 18 participants (mean age 72.00 ± 8.69; 6 [33.33%] females) diagnosed with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) at baseline who progressed to Alzheimer's Disease (AD) at the follow-up, with follow-up assessments conducted at 24.78 ± 1.75 months after baseline.
Longitudinal changes in Axonal Damage (AxD) and Radial Diffusivity (RD) were evaluated using tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) implemented in the FMRIB Software Library (FSL).
Participants with missing baseline or follow-up Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) images were excluded from the study, resulting in the exclusion of 44 participants.
The study included 18 participants with a mean age of 72.00 ± 8.69 and 6 (33.33%) females, classified as APOE ε4 carriers or non-carriers based on allele presence.

Participant classification into cognitively normal, MCI, and AD groups was determined by Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores according to ADNI criteria, with cognitive decline defined as the difference between follow-up and baseline CDR scores over a 2-year period.

Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) data were acquired using a 3T MRI scanner with protocols detailed at https://adni.loni.usc.edu/methods/documents/mri-protocols, and artifacts were corrected using FSL version 6.0.6 and MRtrix3.

Axial diffusivity (AxD) was derived from the primary eigenvalue (λ1), and radial diffusivity (RD) was calculated by averaging the secondary eigenvalues (λ2 and λ3) generated by the 'dtifit' function in FSL.
The primary eigenvalue (λ1) was used to determine the axial diffusivity (AxD), while the secondary eigenvalues (λ2 and λ3) were averaged to derive the radial diffusivity (RD).
The FA maps were registered to an FA template space (FMRIB58_FA 1 × 1 × 1 mm) created using the FA maps of the 18 participants in the study.
A mean FA skeleton was constructed by averaging the FA maps, and a threshold of 0.2 was applied to refine the skeleton to include only voxels with sufficient FA values.

The Johns Hopkins University white-matter tractography atlas was used to create region-of-interest (ROI) masks for the cingulum (CG), corpus callosum (CC), and uncinate fasciculus to extract AxD and RD values.
All statistical analyses were conducted using Jamovi (version 2.3.28.0) and FSL (version 6.0.6).
Permutation testing with 5,000 iterations generated a null distribution of t-values by randomly rearranging the data among the participants.

A threshold-free cluster enhancement method was applied within the permutation-based paired t-tests to correct for multiple comparisons at the voxel level, with statistical significance set at P < 0.05.
A general linear model was incorporated into the TBSS framework with age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status as independent variables and AxD/RD as the dependent variable.

Table 2 lists the specific voxel sizes for significant changes in axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) for 32 distinct white matter regions, including the genu, body, and splenium of the corpus callosum, and the right and left hemispheres of the anterior, superior, and posterior corona radiata.

The largest voxel sizes for increased axial diffusivity (AxD) were observed in the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) and posterior corona radiata (PCR), while widespread increases in AxD and radial diffusivity (RD) were also noted in the internal capsule (IC), corona radiata (CR), and cingulum cingulate gyrus (CG).
The decreased diffusivity metrics (AxD and RD) exhibited no statistically significant differences at P<0.05 after correcting for multiple comparisons using the family-wise error (FWE) method.

The study participants consisted of 6 females (33.33%) and 12 males (66.67%), with an age range of 72.00 (SD 8.69) years at baseline and 74.00 (SD 8.69) years at follow-up. Education levels were distributed as 0 participants with \u22649 years, 2 with 10-12 years, 7 with 13-16 years, and 9 with >16 years.

APOE ε4 carrier status was defined as having \u22651 APOE ε4 alleles, with 6 participants (33.33%) classified as carriers and 12 (66.67%) as non-carriers. The Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score increased from 2.42 ± 1.17 at baseline to 4.64 ± 1.44 at follow-up.

TBSS analysis revealed a significant increase in Axial Diffusivity (AxD) and Radial Diffusivity (RD) values at follow-up compared to baseline across the corpus callosum, internal capsule, corona radiata, thalamic radiation, lateral temporoparietal regions, longitudinal fasciculus, sagittal and external capsule, cingulate gyrus, fornix, and tapetum.

A general linear model was incorporated into the TBSS framework with age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status as independent variables and AxD/RD as the dependent variable. Spearman's correlation analysis examined changes in ROI-based AxD, RD, and CDR while controlling for age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, and baseline CDR score.

Uncorrected P-values were reported for correlation analyses because applying the Bonferroni correction would have significantly lowered statistical power due to the small sample size. A post hoc power analysis was conducted using G*Power version 3.1 to evaluate the adequacy of the sample size in detecting meaningful correlations.

Multiple linear regression analysis evaluated the independent contributions of AxD and RD changes to clinical development, using the change in CDR scores as the dependent variable and AxD and RD as independent variables. Age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, and baseline CDR score were treated as confounders in this regression model.

Multivariate regression analysis was conducted independently for each white matter region that showed notable variations in AxD or RD in the TBSS analysis. Table 1 presents the demographic data for the study participants.

The CDR score increased from a mean of 2.42 ± 1.17 at baseline to 4.64 ± 1.44 at the follow-up over 2 years. Demographic and clinical characteristics were compared between the included group (n=18) and the excluded group (n=44) to assess potential sample bias due to the exclusion of participants with missing DTI data.

No significant differences were found between the included and excluded groups in age (P=0.909), sex (P=0.578), education level (P=0.967), APOE ε4 carrier status (P=0.251), and baseline CDR (P=0.074).

The study reports that axial diffusivity (AxD) changes exhibited the strongest correlation with changes in the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score compared to radial diffusivity (RD) changes. Specific significant correlations for AxD and CDR score changes were found in the left retrolenticular part of the internal capsule (r=0.704, P=0.007), left posterior corona radiata (r=0.676, P=0.011), left fornix cres stria terminalis (r=0.627, P=0.022), and right superior longitudinal fasciculus (r=0.568, P=0.043).

Table 3 provides the complete correlation coefficients (r) and P-values for axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) against Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores for all listed white matter regions, including the corpus callosum, internal capsule, corona radiata, thalamic radiation, cingulum, fornix, fasciculi, and tapetum.
S2 Table summarizes the results of regression analysis for all regions of interest (ROIs).
The study longitudinally evaluated white matter microstructure by analyzing diffusion metrics Axial Diffusivity (AxD) and Radial Diffusivity (RD) measured using Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI).

Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS) analysis revealed significant changes in AxD and RD across the corpus callosum (CC), cingulum (CR), cingulate gyrus (CG), superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF), inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF), and internal capsule (IC).

The study utilized multivariate regression analysis to investigate the separate effects of Axonal Diameter (AxD) and Radial Diffusivity (RD) changes on clinical progression, specifically correlating these metrics with Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores.

AxD changes in the left retrolenticular region of the Internal Capsule (IC), left Posterior Cingulate Region (PCR), left fornix cres stria terminalis, and right Superior Longitudinal Fasciculus (SLF) exhibited significant correlations with changes in CDR scores.

AxD increases in the right SLF, right Sagittal Stratum (SS), left SLF, and left Parietal Tract (PT) showed minor positive trends with CDR changes, although these correlations did not exhibit statistical significance.

The study used G*Power version 3.1 for post hoc power analysis with an alpha of 0.05 and N=18, detecting 93.7% power for a correlation of r=0.704 and 86.3% power for the average observed correlation of r=0.644.

Multiple linear regression analyses used CDR changes as the dependent variable, adjusting for age, APOE epsilon 4 status, education, sex, and baseline CDR to examine the independent contributions of changes in AxD and RD.
AxD changes in the left retrolenticular internal capsule were significantly associated with CDR changes with a beta coefficient of 0.0141 (95% CI [0.0005, 0.0277], P=0.044).

AxD changes in the right superior longitudinal fasciculus (beta 0.0230, P=0.117), right sagittal stratum (beta 0.0157, P=0.152), left superior longitudinal fasciculus (beta 0.0144, P=0.172), and left posterior thalamic radiation (beta 0.0093, P=0.194) exhibited non-significant positive trends with CDR changes.
The regression analysis specifically involved regions of interest exhibiting significant differences in both AxD and RD values in the TBSS analysis, with full results summarized in S2 Table.

The study provides supporting data files S1 and S2, which contain AxD and RD changes in white matter regions of interest for individual participants and ROI-wise multivariate regression analysis of these changes on CDR score changes, respectively, available in XLSX format.
The study provides supporting file S3, a PDF listing the complete acknowledgment of ADNI investigators.
The study used a small sample size of n=18 participants, which limits the generalizability of the findings and reduces statistical power.
Uncorrected p-values were reported due to the small sample size, creating a risk of inflated false-positive rates that requires validation using False Discovery Rate correction in larger samples.
ROI analyses were conducted post hoc based on TBSS findings, which introduces concerns about circular reasoning and necessitates a priori ROI definitions or independent datasets for validation.

Cognitive function was evaluated exclusively using CDR scores, which lack detailed assessment of various cognitive domains and require the incorporation of additional neuropsychological tools like the Montreal Cognitive Assessment or Mini-Mental State Examination.

The TBSS analysis focused only on the core regions of the WM tract by projecting the highest FA values onto the alignment-invariant tract representation, potentially overlooking subtle changes occurring outside the skeleton.

APOE ε4 status was included as a covariate in all statistical models, but potential interaction effects between ε4 status and white matter changes were not tested due to the limited sample size and small number of ε4 carriers.

Standardization across imaging protocols and scanners is necessary to ensure reproducibility of AxD metrics, and normative datasets must be established to define AxD thresholds indicative of pathological changes.

The diffusion tensor model relies on simplified assumptions that may not completely capture the complexity of actual WM structures, necessitating the use of advanced techniques such as neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging or multi-shell DTI.

The primary replication blocker is the absence of subject-level raw data and the specific script used to generate the free-water fraction maps, which prevents independent verification of the reported 'clearer picture' findings.

The absence of confidence intervals for the Free Water effect sizes renders the reported associations uninterpretable regarding clinical significance, as the bounds necessary to distinguish a meaningful shift from noise are missing from the reporting.

Neurite Orientation Density and Dispersion Imaging (NODDI) characterizes brain changes by assuming the diffusion-weighted imaging signal emanates from three distinct tissue compartments: within neurites, outside of neurites, and free water. The primary NODDI parameters are intracellular volume fraction (ICVF), extracellular volume fraction (ECVF), isotropic volume fraction (ISOVF), and orientation dispersion index (ODI).
The study enrolled 43 patients with Alzheimer's disease and 16 healthy controls, and all participants underwent diffusion spectrum imaging (DSI) and conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

The diffusion MRI images were processed to obtain diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI), and mean apparent propagator (MAP) models and multiparameter values.

Pearson correlation analysis was used to assess the relationships between diffusion parameters and clinical cognitive scores, specifically the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores.
Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was conducted to evaluate the diagnostic performance of DTI, NODDI, and MAP parameters for diagnosing Alzheimer's disease.
The study utilizes diffusion spectral imaging (DSI) as a grid acquisition model to reconstruct NODDI, MAP-MRI, and DTI models from raw diffusion data.

The specific MAP-MRI parameters analyzed are return-to-origin probability (RTOP), return-to-axis probability (RTAP), return-to-plane probability (RTPP), mean-squared displacement (MSD), non-Gaussianity (NG), and q-space inverse variance (QIV).
The study assesses correlations between diffusion MRI parameter values and cognitive scores from the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA).
Diagnostic performance of the diffusion MRI parameters is evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves.

The diffusion data analysis pipeline requires converting raw data to NIFTI format, applying eddy current correction using FSL, and denoising with a Gaussian filter with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 3 mm.

The diffusion parameter maps were calculated using in-house prototype software developed by MR Station (Chengdu Zhongying Medical Technology Co., Ltd.), which is not publicly available for replication.
The acquisition protocol involved 24 directions at b=3000 s/mm² and 3 directions at b=0 s/mm², totaling 128 diffusion samples with a scan time of approximately 10 minutes and 8 seconds.
The tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) pipeline was executed within the FSL toolbox from the Oxford Centre for Functional MRI of the Brain (http://fsl.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl/fslwiki/).
Fractional anisotropy (FA) maps for Alzheimer's disease (AD) and healthy controls (HC) were nonlinearly registered to the FMRIB58_FA template.
Affine alignment transformations were applied to all participants to map them into the 1 x 1 x 1 mm^2 Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI152) standard space.
The whole brain was segmented into 50 brain regions using the Johns Hopkins University (JHU)-White Matter-labels as masks.
Nonparametric permutation tests were performed using the randomize tool with 5000 random permutations.
Threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) was used for multiple comparison correction with a statistical threshold defined as p < 0.001.
Statistical analyses were conducted using the IBM SPSS 23.0 software package (IBM Corp, Armonk, NY, USA).
Pearson correlation analysis was implemented with a significance criterion of p < 0.05, and a false discovery rate (FDR) was used to correct for multiple comparisons.

The study enrolled 43 patients with mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease and 16 healthy controls, with 25 of the patients completing both the Mini-Mental Status Examination and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. The diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease was established based on the 2011 National Institute on Aging-Alzheimer's Association diagnostic criteria.

Healthy controls were included if they had no evidence of cognitive impairment, a Mini-Mental Status Examination score of 25 or higher, a Montreal Cognitive Assessment score of 25 or higher, and a Clinical Dementia Rating score of 0. Mild cognitive impairment was defined by subjective cognitive complaint, objective cognitive impairment (at least one test Z value < -1.5), and retention of activities of daily living (ADL scale decrease < 20%).

Alzheimer's disease was defined by progressive episodic memory impairment plus at least one cognitive impairment, indicated by a Clinical Dementia Rating of 1 or higher and a Functional Activities Questionnaire score of 9 or higher. All cases were reviewed by a multidisciplinary consensus panel consisting of a neurologist, neuropsychologist, and neuroradiologist.

Participants were excluded if they had severe cerebrovascular disorder, severe white matter hyperintensity, a history of psychiatric illness or severe injury, used medications that influence cognition, were left-handed, had contraindications to MRI, or had poor-quality MRI images due to movement artifacts. The study was approved by the ethics committee of Zigong First People's Hospital under Ethics (Research) No. 36, 2023.

Diffusion spectrum imaging was acquired on a 3.0T MRI scanner (Skyra; Siemens Healthcare, Erlangen, Germany) equipped with a 32-channel head coil. The sequence parameters were TR/TE = 4400/108 ms, field of view 220 x 220 mm², SMS factor 2, slice thickness 2.0 mm, voxel size 2.0 x 2.0 x 2.0 mm³, and 60 slices.

The diffusion sampling included 128 directions across specific b-values: 0 volumes at b=0 s/mm², 3 directions at b=200 s/mm², 1 direction at b=350 s/mm², 5 directions at b=400 s/mm², 4 directions at b=550 s/mm², 3 directions at b=750 s/mm², 12 directions at b=950 s/mm², 12 directions at b=1150 s/mm², 6 directions at b=1500 s/mm², 15 directions at b=1700 s/mm², 1 direction at b=1850 s/mm², 11 directions at b=1900 s/mm², 12 directions at b=2050 s/mm², 4 directions at b=2250 s/mm², 12 directions at b=2450 s/mm², 24 directions at b=2650 s/mm², and 3 directions at b=3000 s/mm². The total scan time was approximately 10 minutes and 8 seconds.

The study included 43 AD patients and 16 healthy volunteers, with the AD group having a significantly higher average age and significantly lower years of education, MMSE scores, and MoCA scores compared to the healthy control group.

Statistical analysis used a significance level of p<0.05 and false discovery rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons, with regression models adjusted for the square of age, gender, and years of education.

Diagnostic performance of diffusion parameter values in distinguishing AD was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC) analysis to calculate sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and area under the curve (AUC) in SPSS.

In the DTI model, the AD group showed significantly higher AxD, MD, and RD values in the body of the corpus callosum, splenium of the corpus callosum, and anterior corona radiata R/L compared to the healthy control group.

In the DTI model, the AD group showed notably decreased FA values in the middle cerebellar peduncle, genu of corpus callosum, body of corpus callosum, splenium of corpus callosum, anterior corona radiata R/L, and superior longitudinal fasciculus R/L compared to the healthy control group.

In the NODDI model, the AD group had significantly higher ECVF values in the genu of corpus callosum, body of corpus callosum, splenium of corpus callosum, and anterior corona radiata R/L compared to the healthy control group.

The ICVF values in the splenium of the corpus callosum showed the strongest correlation with MoCA scores (r=0.649, p<0.001). No ECVF, ODI, or ISOVF values for any fiber were significantly correlated with the MoCA scores.

The RTAP values in the stria terminalis R (r=0.737, p<0.001) and the RTOP values in the stria terminalis R (r=0.734, p<0.001) exhibited the strongest correlation with MMSE scores. The RTAP values in the stria terminalis R (r=0.699, p<0.001) and the RTOP values in the cerebral peduncle R (r=0.717, p<0.001) exhibited the strongest correlation with MoCA scores.

DTI radial diffusivity (DTI-RD) exhibited the best diagnostic performance for AD or MCI in the splenium of the corpus callosum (AUC=0.86, 95% CI 0.76-0.95), fornix (AUC=0.93, 95% CI 0.86-1.00), right cerebral peduncle (AUC=0.95, 95% CI 0.91-1.00), left cerebral peduncle (AUC=0.88, 95% CI 0.79-0.97), and right stria terminalis (AUC=0.92, 95% CI 0.84-0.99).
The DTI mean diffusivity (DTI-MD) parameter demonstrated the best diagnostic performance in the right anterior corona radiata (AUC=0.92, p=0.005).

The study analyzed correlations between DTI-derived parameters (AxD, FA, MD, RD), NODDI-derived parameters (ECVF, ICVF, ISOVF), and MAP-MRI-derived parameters (MSD, QIV, NG, NGAx, NGRad, RTAP, RTOP, RTPP) with MMSE and MoCA scores in 25 Alzheimer's disease patients.

Fractional anisotropy (FA) values in the fornix (r=0.740, p<0.001), anterior corona radiata left (r=0.617, p<0.001), and stria terminalis right (r=0.715, p<0.001) showed strong positive correlations with MMSE scores.

Fractional anisotropy (FA) values in the fornix (r=0.690, p<0.001), stria terminalis right (r=0.644, p<0.001), and stria terminalis left (r=0.617, p<0.001) demonstrated strong positive correlations with MoCA scores.

NODDI-derived extracellular volume fraction (ECVF) in the anterior corona radiata right (r=0.642, p<0.001), intracellular volume fraction (ICVF) in the splenium of the corpus callosum (r=0.666, p<0.001), and isotropic volume fraction (ISOVF) in the stria terminalis right (r=0.604, p<0.001) exhibited the strongest correlations with MMSE scores.

The study cohort consisted of 43 Alzheimer's disease patients (mean age 72.86 ± 8.23 years, 17 male/26 female, median education 9 years) and 16 healthy controls (mean age 65.81 ± 8.50 years, 7 male/9 female, median education 11 years).

Neuropsychologic scores for the 25 Alzheimer's disease patients with available data showed a median Mini-Mental State Examination score of 6 (interquartile range 3-14) and a median Montreal Cognitive Assessment score of 3 (interquartile range 0-8.50).

The diffusion imaging analysis utilized specific parameters: axial diffusivity, fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity, and radial diffusivity from DTI; extracellular volume fraction, intracellular volume fraction, and isotropic volume fraction from NODDI; and mean-squared displacement, non-Gaussianity, axial non-Gaussianity, radial non-Gaussianity, q-space inverse variance, return-to-origin probability, return-to-axis probability, and return-to-plane probability from MAP-MRI.

Statistical significance for the diffusion parameter maps was defined as P < 0.001, with red indicating increased parameter values and blue indicating decreased parameter values in the Alzheimer's disease group compared to the healthy control group.

In the Alzheimer's disease group, isotropic volume fraction values were significantly increased in the body of corpus callosum, splenium of corpus callosum, external capsule, and cerebral peduncle compared to the healthy control group.

In the Alzheimer's disease group, mean-squared displacement and q-space inverse variance values were significantly higher than in the healthy control group in the frontal lobe, occipital parietal lobe, cerebral peduncle, and corpus callosum.

In the Alzheimer's disease group, radial non-Gaussianity, return-to-axis probability, return-to-origin probability, and return-to-plane probability values were significantly lower than in the healthy control group in the genu of corpus callosum, body of corpus callosum, splenium of corpus callosum, anterior corona radiata, and superior corona radiata.
The Delong's test comparing the AUC of MAP-RTOP and NODDI-ECVF in the right anterior corona radiata yielded a Z-score of -2.217 and a p-value of 0.027.

The standardized beta coefficients (β*) reported in the diagnostic performance table for diffusion imaging parameters in Alzheimer's disease patients are specific statistical outputs required to replicate the model coefficients.
The datasets used and/or analyzed during the study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.
The study lacked positron emission tomography (PET) examinations or pathologic verification confirming tau protein deposition in participants with Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment.
The Alzheimer's disease groups were not divided into various subtypes due to the relatively small sample size, limiting the wide applicability of the results.
The analysis did not consider the presence of white matter hyperintensities (WMH), which may have influenced results due to heterogeneous macrostructural white matter impairments across participants.

The study evaluated the NODDI model and identified that the lack of significant ODI differences between the HC and AD groups may arise from the inherent limitations of the Watson distribution used in NODDI modeling.

The Watson distribution used in NODDI modeling has diminished accuracy in complex brain regions such as kissing fibers, crossing axons requiring higher-order spherical harmonics, and regions with diffuse pathological changes involving bidirectional effects from dendritic pruning and neurite beading.
The DTI model assumes that the diffusion of water molecules in the brain follows a Gaussian distribution, which limits its ability to detect the diffusion heterogeneity of brain tissue.

MAP-MRI metrics are characterized by their direct correlation with microstructural features and their ability to characterize non-Gaussian diffusion profiles, which reflects more complex tissue organization compared to NODDI.
The research involving human subjects was approved by the Ethics Committee of Zigong First People's Hospital under protocol number Ethics(Reseach) No. 36, 2023.

The corresponding author for the study is Zhongjianquan, reachable at zhongjianquan.2010@qq.com, and the work was conducted by researchers from the Department of Radiology and Department of Neurology at Zigong First People's Hospital in Zigong, Sichuan, China.

The study utilized the Free-Water implementation within the FSL EDIFY module but omitted the specific thresholding parameters for fiber orientation distribution estimation, which are required to reproduce the reported 84% atlas coverage and cluster sizes.
Reproduction of the Free-Water DTI pipeline is blocked by the absence of the specific FSL EDIFY software version and the exact thresholding values used for acquisition and post-processing.

Reproducing the Free-Water DTI analysis requires the exact exclusion criteria used to remove 44 participants, the specific version of FSL EDIFY, and the step-by-step processing log, as these are currently missing and block verification of the 18-participant sample.

The three studies under review utilize distinct methodological frameworks without providing harmonized data access, standardized software versions, or shared processing logs, which blocks the execution of a unified replication pipeline.

Independent verification of the region-of-interest selection is currently blocked because the exact coordinate files for the a priori ROIs, the specific mask files, the thresholding parameters for the initial whole-brain scan, and the version of the tractography software are missing from the provided materials.

The small sample size and lack of independent validation prevent the Free-Water DTI method from being replicated as a reliable diagnostic tool, as there is insufficient data to distinguish true pathology from noise or false positives. The current findings function only as a hypothesis-generating snapshot rather than a validated protocol with reproducible clinical specificity.

Independent verification of the statistical results is blocked because the report omits 95% confidence intervals, exact p-values, and the specific multiple comparison correction method, leaving the family-wise error rate uncorrected.

The post hoc ROI selection creates a circularity that prevents the replication from testing a new hypothesis, meaning any re-run would merely reproduce the original study's specific methodological errors rather than validating the Free-Water signal.

To reproduce the analysis, the specific cognitive test battery identifiers used to derive the final CDR scores and the unprocessed raw longitudinal diffusion maps are required to verify if the clinical decline aligns with the imaging trajectory.

Replication of the Free-Water correction analysis is blocked by the absence of raw diffusion data and specific software versions, which are necessary to confirm if the detected signal is robust or an artifact of the small sample size.

A multi-site longitudinal trial requires a minimum sample size of 120 participants per group to achieve 80% statistical power for detecting a moderate effect size, which is a necessary condition for distinguishing the Free-Water metric from noise.

Reproduction of the statistical analysis must include a False Discovery Rate correction to control the Type I error rate, as this specific guardrail is required to prevent the Free-Water signal from being indistinguishable from small-sample artifacts.

The acquisition parameters of the original studies, specifically a b-value of 1000 s/mm² with only 30 directions, are insufficient for reliable compartmental modeling of the Free-Water metric, creating a data gap that forces the fitting algorithm to rely on Gaussian assumptions.

documents: ## scientific reports OPEN Free-water diffusion tensor imaging improves the accuracy and sensitivity of white matter analysis in Alzheimer's disease

## scientific reports OPEN Free-water diffusion tensor imaging improves the accuracy and sensitivity of white matter analysis in Alzheimer's disease Maurizio Bergamino ${ }^{\mathbf{1}}$, Ryan R. Walsh ${ }^{\mathbf{2}}$ \& Ashley M. Stokes ${ }^{\mathbf{1}}$
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) based diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) can assess white matter (WM) integrity through several metrics, such as fractional anisotropy (FA), axial/radial diffusivities (AxD/RD), and mode of anisotropy (MA). Standard DTI is susceptible to the effects of extracellular free water (FW), which can be removed using an advanced free-water DTI (FW-DTI) model. The purpose of this study was to compare standard and FW-DTI metrics in the context of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Data were obtained from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) database and included both healthy controls (HC) and mild-to-moderate AD. With both standard and FW-DTI, decreased FA was found in AD, mainly in the corpus callosum and fornix, consistent with neurodegenerative mechanisms. Widespread higher AxD and RD were observed with standard DTI; however, the FW index, indicative of AD-associated neurodegeneration, was significantly elevated in these regions in AD, highlighting the potential impact of free water contributions on standard DTI in neurodegenerative pathologies. Using FW-DTI, improved consistency was observed in FA, AxD, and RD, and the complementary FW index was higher in the AD group as expected. With both standard and FW-DTI, higher values of MA coupled with higher values of FA in AD were found in the anterior thalamic radiation and cortico-spinal tract, most likely arising from a loss of crossing fibers. In conclusion, FW-DTI better reflects the underlying pathology of AD and improves the accuracy of DTI metrics related to WM integrity in Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder and the most common cause of dementia in older adults ${ }^{1}$. Current biomarkers for AD target the dominant pathological paradigm, characterized by beta-amyloid and tau pathologies, as well as neurodegenerative changes. While much of the pathologic evidence of AD is found in gray matter, it is well recognized that concomitant white matter (WM) alterations occur in the brains of AD populations, suggesting an expanded role for WM-based biomarkers in $\mathrm{AD}^{2}$.

nd in gray matter, it is well recognized that concomitant white matter (WM) alterations occur in the brains of AD populations, suggesting an expanded role for WM-based biomarkers in $\mathrm{AD}^{2}$. Diffusion-based magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) enables the in vivo evaluation of brain microstructure and, more specifically, WM integrity by probing water diffusivity associated with axons ${ }^{3}$; most commonly, diffusion-related parameters are obtained by analysis using the diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) model. In WM, faster diffusivity along the fibers, with lower perpendicular diffusivity, yields a higher fractional anisotropy (FA). While decreased FA has been associated with demyelination, edema, gliosis, and inflammation, FA is unfortunately an indirect marker of WM integrity because the individual microscopic contributions of various non-WM components cannot be disentangled ${ }^{4,5}$. Other DTI-derived metrics include axial diffusivity (AxD), which may be related to axonal damage, and radial diffusivity (RD), which is correlated with myelin integrity, axonal diameter and density, and fiber coherence ${ }^{6}$. Prior DTI studies have shown that AD is associated with lower FA and higher AxD and RD values across multiple regions in the WM, including the corpus callosum (CC), fornix, cingulum, inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF), and superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) ${ }^{7-9}$. Moreover, changes in DTI metrics may precede both neuronal loss and symptoms onset, suggesting their potential role as early biomarkers. While several studies have shown a correlation between DTI-derived metrics and cognitive scores ${ }^{10-12}$, other similar investigations have failed to show a significant correlation ${ }^{13-16}$ suggesting methodologic and/or analytic impacts on dMRI-derived data.

Although dMRI is a well-recognized method for assessing WM, it has several limitations, including known inaccuracies related to partial volume effects (PVEs), wherein the resulting DTI metrics reflect a weighted average of multiple diffusion components within a voxel and are thus no longer specific to a single tissue type ${ }^{17}$. The impact of PVEs may be particularly profound in AD, where neuronal loss leads to secondary ex vacuo increases in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and free water (FW) across the brain. To overcome the effects of extracellular FW on DTI-derived metrics, a FW correction algorithm has been developed to quantify and remove the contribution of extracellular FW ${ }^{18}$. FW-DTI has been shown to improve both tissue specificity ${ }^{19}$ and DTI-based tract reconstruction ${ }^{18}$. This model has previously been used to study several neurological diseases, including AD ${ }^{20-24}$, Parkinson's disease ${ }^{25}$, and depression ${ }^{26,27}$.

This model has previously been used to study several neurological diseases, including AD ${ }^{20-24}$, Parkinson's disease ${ }^{25}$, and depression ${ }^{26,27}$. Using FW-DTI in a healthy aging population enriched for AD risk, Hoy et al. found that DTI-based markers of altered microstructure were significantly associated with CSF biomarkers of preclinical AD pathology ${ }^{20}$. FW correction may be particularly important in the fornix, due to both its proximity to the lateral ventricles and its association with the hippocampus ${ }^{22}$, and may also improve sensitivity to conversion to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) relative to uncorrected DTI metrics ${ }^{23}$. The FW index has separately been proposed as a standalone biomarker of AD-related pathology. This index has been associated with cognitive decline in multiple domains and may enable separation of vascular and neurodegenerative contributions to cognitive decline in the presence of mixed dementia ${ }^{21}$. More recently, an elevated FW index was observed in MCI and AD patients compared with healthy controls (HC), even after correction for white matter hyperintensities ${ }^{28}$. However, none of these studies have directly compared standard and FW-DTI metrics in the context of distinguishing between AD and HC. As AD-related WM degeneration leads to a significant intravoxel FW component, FW-DTI may improve sensitivity to early brain changes and provide a clearer and more specific interpretation of results compared to standard DTI.

In this study, we compared FA, AxD, RD, and MA from both standard DTI and FW-DTI between AD and HC subjects obtained from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) brain project ${ }^{29}$. This dataset was previously used to investigate AD-related changes in the size and shape of the $\mathrm{CC}^{30,31}$. We also investigated the complementary FW index for both groups and analyzed voxel-based correlations between all DTI-derived metrics (from DTI and FW-DTI) and the mini-mental state examination (MMSE) score ${ }^{32}$. We hypothesize that FW-DTI will improve the sensitivity and specificity for detection of WM tract abnormalities in AD. More specifically, increased FW due to neurodegeneration reduces the accuracy of diffusion-derived metrics, and thus, the removal of FW contributions improves the estimation of DTI metrics and may increase confidence in the patterns observed across DTI studies. In addition, the ability to quantify FW may yield complementary insight into sub-voxel WM neurodegenerative processes. The application of FW-DTI for AD better reflects the underlying pathology and should thus further improve interpretation of AD WM pathology.

All data were downloaded from the OASIS-3 brain project (http://oasis-brains.org/), which is a neuroimaging dataset for normal aging and Alzheimer's disease and is freely available to the scientific community. Inclusion criteria were participants between the ages of 60 and 90 years who had 3 T dMRI data available with more than 30 directions. Exclusion criteria were cognitively impaired participants with dementia not attributed to AD, healthy control participants with significant comorbidities, and participants for whom the MMSE was not available. Only one time-point was used per subject. Subsequently, this study included 30 HCs (17 females; age (standard deviation, S.D.) = 73 (6) years) and 28 AD subjects (primarily mild AD; 15 females; age $=75$ (7) years). Four AD subjects had remote mood disorders and one had a remote hypothyroidism as secondary medical diagnoses. The Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) ${ }^{33}$, which is a 5-point scale used to characterize multiple domains of cognitive and functional abilities, was zero for all HCs and between 0.5 and 3.0 for the AD group. The MMSE is a 30-point assessment commonly used to measure cognitive impairment. The mean value of MMSE was 29.10 (S.D. 1.24) for HC and 24.18 (S.D. 5.02) for AD. All subject characteristics are summarized in Table 1.

For all subjects, the acquisition was performed using 64 diffusion-encoding directions (b value:

Data preprocessing. DMRI data were downloaded in NIFTI format and processed as previously described ${ }^{26,27}$. Briefly, the data were preprocessed using the functional magnetic resonance imaging of the brain (FMRIB) software library tool (FSL, version 5.0.4) ${ }^{34}$. Following translation and rotation estimation, the raw dMRI images were corrected for eddy currents and motion ${ }^{35}$. After motion correction, the gradient orientations were compensated (prior to calculating B-matrices) to account for the rotational component of registration. A brain mask was defined for each subject using the Brain Extraction Toolbox (BET) ${ }^{36}$ for the single B0 images. DTI standard (uncorrected for FW) and FW-corrected maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script ${ }^{26}$, which is available upon request. The FW maps were computed by fitting the following model at each voxel ${ }^{18}$ :

FW maps were computed by fitting the following model at each voxel ${ }^{18}$ : $$
A_{g}(D, f)=f \cdot\left(\exp \left[-b g^{T} D g\right]\right)+(1-f) \cdot \exp \left[-b D_{\text {water }}\right]
$$ where $A_{g}$ is the modeled attenuated signal (normalized by B0) for the applied diffusion gradient $g$, and $b$ is the b-value $\left(1000 \mathrm{~s} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}\right)$. The first term reflects the tissue compartment, where $D$ is the diffusion tensor of this compartment, $f$ is the fractional volume of the compartment, and $g^{T}$ is the transpose of the vector $g$. The second term reflects an isotropic free-water compartment with a fractional volume of $(1-f)$, where the diffusion coefficient $D_{\text {water }}$ is set to the diffusivity of water at body temperature $\left(3 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~mm}^{2} / \mathrm{s}\right)$. The B0 group-wise template image was subsequently normalized to the IIT_mean_b0 image by ANTs symmetric image normalization (SyN) algorithm ${ }^{39}$. The warp fields obtained from this normalization and from the B0 group-wise template creation were used to transfer all DTI maps (standard and FW-corrected) to the Illinois Institute of Technology (IIT) Human Brain Atlas (v.4.1), which contains both anatomical and DTI brain templates in International Consortium for Brain Mapping (ICBM)-152 space ${ }^{40}$. Age, MMSE, and CDR scores are presented as mean and standard deviation (SD) for each group. Differences in age, sex, and cognitive test scores between groups were assessed using the Student's t-test. Comparisons of all DTI-, FW-DTI- metrics, and FW maps between groups were performed using the FSL Randomise tool ${ }^{41}$ with threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) ${ }^{42}$ and a correction for multiple comparisons via Family-Wise Error (FWE) rate ${ }^{38}$ at a 0.01 level. A WM mask was defined using a threshold of 0.2 on the average values of FA (from standard DTI) and was applied to the other DTI maps. For each voxel, the DTI-derived metrics were fitted by an Analysis of Covariance model (ANCOVA), which included age and sex as covariates. The number of randomized permutations was set at 5,000. The clusters identified to be statistically different between groups were labeled according to the JHU DTI-based white-matter atlases ${ }^{43,44}$. All results are reported with a significance threshold of $p$ value < 0.01, corrected for FWE, except where otherwise noted.

Although DTI is a commonly used method for assessing WM, PVEs can reduce the accuracy of DTI metrics, ultimately limiting their interpretation. To mitigate PVE, free water-contaminated voxels were removed by incorporating a FW component in the conventional diffusion modeling pipeline ${ }^{18}$, producing more accurate FW-corrected DTI metrics and the complementary FW index. Using both standard and FW-DTI, significant WM differences were observed between HC and AD subjects in several regions, including both higher and lower FA. Both AxD and RD were highly impacted by the effects of FW, and FW-corrected AxDt and RDt were more consistent with pathology-based expected spatial patterns of neurodegeneration. The FW index was higher in AD than HC across many regions, as expected. The FW correction method has shown promise in many neurological diseases of the $\mathrm{WM}^{21,24-27}$, particularly those with neurodegenerative aspects; similarly, we now demonstrate that the application of FW correction in AD improves the accuracy and sensitivity of the resulting DTI metrics.
